lessons.title: A world inside a cell

lead.text: Look at the animal cell and the bacterium. Each is a tiny bag, yet food and waste cross its outline all the time.

reveal.text: You named the boundary both cells share: the plasma membrane, also called the cell membrane. It lets some substances through and holds others back.

steps.headline: Eukaryotic cells keep their DNA in a nucleus. Bacteria keep theirs in a nucleoid.

lead.text: Cells come in two designs. Animal and plant cells are eukaryotic: a nucleus, wrapped in its own membrane, holds most of the DNA.
A bacterium has no nucleus. Its DNA lies in a region called the nucleoid, with no membrane round it.

steps.headline: Where is the DNA in a leaf cell?

workedSteps.text: Look for a compartment with its own membrane.
The leaf cell has one: the nucleus. Most of its DNA is inside.

steps.headline: Where is the DNA in a bacterium?

workedSteps.text: Look for a nucleus.
The bacterium has none.
Its DNA is still there.

steps.headline: Organelles are the parts of a eukaryotic cell, and each has a job.

lead.text: Inside a eukaryotic cell, organelles share out the work.
Mitochondria transfer energy from fuel into a form the cell can use. Chloroplasts capture light energy in leaf cells. Ribosomes build proteins.
A leaf cell makes sugar in the light. After dark there is no light, yet the cell still needs energy.

reveal.text: A leaf cell holds both organelles. Chloroplasts handle light, and mitochondria handle fuel, so having one never replaces the other.

lead.text: Plants have no skeleton, yet a leaf stands up. Something outside each cell's membrane helps it hold its shape.

reveal.text: A plant cell wall lies outside the plasma membrane and helps the cell resist expansion. The membrane still controls exchange.

lessons.orientation: Connect cell structures to their jobs and distinguish bacteria from eukaryotes.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A cell is alive. All day long it needs food coming in and waste going out.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell a bacterium from an animal or plant cell, and match each main structure to its job.
intro.whyItMatters: Every later idea in biology happens inside these cells.

recap.keyIdea: Every cell has a plasma membrane. Eukaryotic cells also have a nucleus and organelles with jobs, while a bacterium keeps its DNA in a nucleoid.

blocks.text: You named the plasma membrane both cells share, found the DNA in a leaf cell's nucleus and in a bacterium's nucleoid, and matched mitochondria and chloroplasts to their jobs.

recap.nextHook: Everything that crosses that membrane has to move somehow. Which way will molecules go?

lessons.title: Which way will molecules move?

steps.headline: Diffusion is the net movement of a substance from where it is crowded to where it is not.

lead.text: A solute is a dissolved substance. Its particles move at random, so some cross a gap each way. More particles cross from the crowded side, and the difference is the net movement.
When concentrations are equal, the flows match. That balance is equilibrium.
Here is the same idea on a membrane. Compare how crowded each side is, then think about which way more particles cross.

reveal.text: You predicted the direction of net movement: from the more concentrated side to the less concentrated side. Individual particles still cross both ways.

steps.headline: Equal volumes hold 9 and 3 units of freely crossing solute. How many units are on each side at equilibrium?

workedSteps.text: Add the two sides.
Solute only moves, so the total is fixed.
Then split it between two equal volumes.

steps.headline: Equal volumes hold 10 and 6 units. How many are on each side at equilibrium?

workedSteps.text: Add the two sides.
Share the total between the two equal volumes.

steps.headline: A membrane only passes the substances it is permeable to.

lead.text: Membranes are selective. A membrane is permeable to a substance if that substance can cross it, and impermeable if it cannot.
Always check this before you predict any movement.
Compare the two cases on the screen. Ask what can cross in each before you follow any difference in concentration.

reveal.text: You checked permeability before following the gradient. When a substance cannot cross, the difference in concentration moves nothing.

lead.text: At equilibrium nothing seems to change. Yet particles keep crossing, in both directions, at the same average rate.

reveal.text: Equal concentrations mean no net movement, not no solute. Diffusion moves solute around and never destroys it.

lessons.orientation: Predict net diffusion from concentration and membrane permeability.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Two equal rooms are joined by an open door. 20 people stand in the left room and 4 in the right.
Everyone wanders at random, in any direction, through the door.

intro.promise: By the end you'll predict which way a dissolved substance moves across a membrane, and when it will not move at all.
intro.whyItMatters: It explains how cells take in nutrients without spending energy.

recap.keyIdea: A solute that can cross a membrane moves net from the crowded side to the sparse side until the concentrations match. A solute that cannot cross stays put.

blocks.text: You shared 24 people between two equal rooms and 16 solute units between two equal compartments. The totals did not change. A blocked solute kept its starting amount.

recap.nextHook: Water can cross a membrane that solute cannot. Which way does the water go?

lessons.title: When only water can cross

steps.headline: Concentration is solute per volume, so adding water lowers it.

lead.text: Concentration is the amount of solute divided by the volume it is dissolved in.
Change the volume and the concentration changes, even when the amount of solute does not.
This membrane is selective: water can cross, but solute cannot. Compare how much solute each side holds.

reveal.text: You followed the water to the more concentrated side. That movement has a name: osmosis.

steps.headline: Osmosis is the net movement of water toward the side with more solute.

lead.text: A membrane that passes water but not solute is selectively permeable. Water crosses both ways, but more crosses toward the side with more solute.
The solute stays where it is, so the volumes change.

steps.headline: A compartment holds 6 solute units in volume 2. Water enters until its volume is 3. How does the concentration change?

workedSteps.text: Before: amount divided by volume.
The solute cannot cross, so the amount stays at 6.
After: use the new volume.

steps.headline: A compartment holds 12 solute units in volume 2. What is its concentration?

workedSteps.text: Identify the amount of solute: 12 units.
Divide by the volume.

lead.text: Use the same moves as before. Ask what stays fixed when water crosses and what changes.

reveal.text: The solute amount did not move, and only the volume did. The concentration followed the volume.

lead.text: Our model has nothing pushing back. A real plant cell has a wall round its membrane, and it swells against that wall as water enters.

reveal.text: Water movement depends on pressure as well as solute concentration. The simple model leaves pressure out.

lessons.orientation: Predict osmosis without confusing solute amount with concentration.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A jug holds 6 spoonfuls of syrup in 2 litres of drink.
You top it up with water, adding no more syrup, until it holds 4 litres.

intro.promise: By the end you'll predict which way water moves across a membrane when solute cannot, and work out how concentrations change.
intro.whyItMatters: It is why a lettuce leaf crisps in water and wilts in salt.

recap.keyIdea: When only water can cross a membrane, it moves toward the side with more solute. The solute stays put, so volumes and concentrations change.

blocks.text: You diluted a drink, followed water toward the more concentrated side, and worked out new concentrations as the volume changed.

recap.nextHook: Enzymes are proteins that speed up reactions. How do you tell what they actually do from data?

lessons.title: Make a reaction easier

steps.headline: An enzyme speeds a reaction by lowering its energy barrier, and it is not used up.

lead.text: A reaction needs a push to get started. That push is its activation energy.
An enzyme is a protein that lowers this barrier, so the reaction runs faster. The enzyme comes out unchanged and can work again.
Enzymes are proteins, and proteins are sensitive. Think about what a hot oven does to an egg.

reveal.text: At 55°C the rate drops to 3 units per minute. You predicted the fall: too much heat damages the enzyme.

steps.headline: An enzyme works because its shape fits its substrate. Heat can spoil the fit.

lead.text: The substrate is the molecule an enzyme acts on. It binds at the enzyme's active site, which has a matching shape.
Too much heat changes that shape. The enzyme is then denatured and works badly.

steps.headline: Enzyme B's rates at 10, 25, 40 and 55°C are 1, 3, 7 and 11 units per minute. Which temperature gave the highest rate?

workedSteps.text: List each rate against its temperature.
The largest rate is 11, at 55°C.
Enzyme B is still rising at 55°C, so its best temperature may be higher still.

steps.headline: Now read Enzyme A: 2, 8, 12 and 3 units per minute at 10, 25, 40 and 55°C.

workedSteps.text: List each rate against its temperature.
Pick the largest.

lead.text: Each enzyme molecule handles one substrate molecule at a time. Adding substrate raises the rate only while active sites are free.

reveal.text: You found the limit: the amount of enzyme. Adding substrate cannot help once every active site is busy.

lead.text: To test an enzyme fairly, run a matched control: the same mixture and conditions, with no enzyme.

reveal.text: The control makes the comparison fair. The difference between the two samples is the enzyme's effect.

lessons.orientation: Read enzyme data and distinguish catalysis, saturation and fair comparisons.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Two beakers run the same reaction. Beaker A makes 4 units of product each minute.
Beaker B holds a helper molecule and makes 12 units each minute.

intro.promise: By the end you'll say what an enzyme does, read enzyme data, and judge whether an experiment tests the enzyme fairly.
intro.whyItMatters: Every reaction in your body runs at the speed it does because of enzymes.

recap.keyIdea: An enzyme lowers a reaction's activation energy. Its effect depends on its shape and its amount, and a matched control shows what it did.

blocks.text: You found that beaker B ran three times faster, picked the best temperature from data, and measured an enzyme's effect against a matched control.

recap.nextHook: Plants build sugar from air. Where does a leaf get its carbon?

lessons.title: Where does a leaf get its carbon?

lead.text: Sugar is built from carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms. Follow the atoms, not the energy.

reveal.text: You traced the carbon to carbon dioxide. Light provides energy, but it does not supply atoms.

steps.headline: Photosynthesis builds glucose from carbon dioxide and water, using light energy.

lead.text: Written simply: 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂.
The sugar is glucose. The numbers in front say how many molecules react, and oxygen leaves as a product.

steps.headline: How many CO₂ molecules must be taken in to make five glucose molecules?

workedSteps.text: One glucose holds six carbon atoms.
Five glucose hold five lots of six.
Each CO₂ brings in one carbon atom, so count them.

steps.headline: How many CO₂ molecules supply the carbon for two glucose molecules?

workedSteps.text: One glucose holds six carbon atoms.
Two glucose hold twice as many.
Each CO₂ brings in one carbon atom.

steps.headline: Light brings energy and no matter. The plant stores it in sugar and later releases it.

lead.text: Photosynthesis captures some light energy and stores it in the bonds of glucose.
Cells can later use that sugar as fuel, in a process called respiration. Plants do both.
A leaf cell has chloroplasts, but that does not make it self-sufficient. At night it still has work to do.

reveal.text: Chloroplasts store energy in sugar. Respiration is what releases it for the cell's work, so a leaf cell needs both.

lead.text: A leaf was given a fixed, low supply of CO₂. Its rate was measured at several light levels. Compare two readings to see what extra light did.

reveal.text: The rate did not change, so light was not what limited it. With so little CO₂, the CO₂ supply set the rate.

lessons.orientation: Trace carbon and energy through the overall photosynthesis reaction.
lessons.reviewLabel: Where does a leaf get its carbon?
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A sapling weighs 2 kg when it is planted in a tub of soil.
Years later it weighs 77 kg. The soil has lost only 60 grams.

intro.promise: By the end you'll say where a leaf's carbon comes from, use the photosynthesis equation to count molecules, and keep matter and energy apart.
intro.whyItMatters: Nearly all the food and fuel we use started as sugar made this way.

recap.keyIdea: Photosynthesis builds sugar from carbon dioxide and water. Light supplies the energy, which the plant stores in the sugar.

blocks.text: You traced a tree's mass to the air and water, then counted CO₂, water and oxygen molecules for several glucose molecules.
You also read a flat curve as a limit set by something other than light.

recap.nextHook: A cell burns sugar to do its work. How does it use that fuel?

lessons.title: How does a cell use its fuel?

steps.headline: Cells transfer energy from fuel into ATP, then spend ATP on their work.

lead.text: Respiration is a set of chemical reactions that transfer energy from fuel such as glucose.
Much of that energy goes into ATP, a small molecule that cells spend on work. The rest disperses as heat. Using oxygen is called aerobic respiration.
Plants make sugar only when there is light. Yet they are alive around the clock, and living cells always have work to do.

reveal.text: You named the process that runs on stored fuel. It needs no light, so it carries on in the dark.

steps.headline: Complete aerobic oxidation of three glucose molecules produces how many CO₂ molecules?

workedSteps.text: One glucose holds six carbon atoms.
Three glucose hold three lots of six.
Each carbon atom ends up in one CO₂, so there are 18.

steps.headline: Complete aerobic oxidation of two glucose molecules produces how many CO₂ molecules?

workedSteps.text: One glucose holds six carbon atoms.
Each carbon atom ends up in one CO₂.

steps.headline: Breathing moves air. Cellular respiration is the chemistry that goes on in cells.

lead.text: Breathing brings oxygen in and carries carbon dioxide out. Cellular respiration is what happens inside cells: reactions that use that oxygen and the fuel.
The two are linked, but they are different things.
Respiring organisms in a sealed jar use oxygen, so the oxygen amount falls. Measure it at the start and again later.

reveal.text: You measured respiration by the oxygen that disappeared. The same method works for any living material in a sealed jar.

lead.text: Careful experimenters also set up a blank: an identical jar with no organisms. It shows what the apparatus does by itself.

reveal.text: The blank separated the organisms' use from the apparatus's. Without it, the whole drop would have been credited to the organisms.

lessons.orientation: Connect respiration, ATP and conserved atoms without confusing breathing with cellular reactions.
lessons.reviewLabel: How does a cell use its fuel?
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A candle burns wax with oxygen. It gives out heat, light, carbon dioxide and water vapour.
Your cells treat sugar in a similar way, without any flame.

intro.promise: By the end you'll say how a cell transfers energy from fuel and follow its carbon atoms, and tell breathing from respiration.
intro.whyItMatters: It explains why you need food and oxygen, and why you breathe out carbon dioxide.

recap.keyIdea: Respiration transfers energy from fuel into ATP, and conserves the fuel's atoms in its products. Breathing is not the same thing.

blocks.text: You counted the CO₂ that two and then three glucose molecules produce.
You also measured oxygen use in a sealed jar and removed the blank's loss from the total.

recap.nextHook: Cells must copy their DNA before they divide. How does a cell copy a message one base at a time?

lessons.title: Copy a message one base at a time

steps.headline: A DNA strand is a row of bases, and each base pairs with only one partner.

lead.text: A strand is a row of four kinds of base: A, T, C and G. A always pairs with T, and C always pairs with G.
So one strand fixes the other. Each strand is a template for its complementary partner.

steps.headline: Write the partner of the strand 5′-GATC-3′.

workedSteps.text: Pair each base with its partner.
Write the partners beneath, left to right.
The partner runs the opposite way along the molecule.

steps.headline: Write the partner bases beneath 5′-AAGC-3′.

workedSteps.text: A pairs with T, so the first partner base is T.
Pair the rest, left to right.

steps.headline: Replication is semiconservative: each new molecule keeps one old strand.

lead.text: To copy DNA, the two strands separate. Each one acts as a template for a new partner.
Every new molecule is half old and half new.
Think of the unzipped strips again. After one round of copying, count the molecules that are zipped together.

reveal.text: You counted two molecules. Each took one old strand and built a new partner for it.

steps.headline: After copying, a chromosome is two joined copies. It is still one chromosome.

lead.text: A chromosome is one long DNA molecule with its proteins. Replication copies it.
The identical copies stay joined and are called sister chromatids. Together they count as one chromosome.
Copying has just happened in a cell. Its DNA amount has changed, but ask what has happened to the number of chromosomes.

reveal.text: The DNA doubled, but the chromosomes did not. Each one now has two sister chromatids.

lessons.orientation: Use complementary DNA bases and distinguish DNA amount from chromosome count.
lessons.reviewLabel: Copy a message one base at a time
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Two strips are zipped together. You unzip them, and give each loose strip a brand-new partner that fits it exactly.

intro.promise: By the end you'll copy a DNA strand base by base and say what each new molecule keeps.
intro.whyItMatters: Every new cell needs a complete copy of the instructions.

recap.keyIdea: Each strand of DNA is a template, so each new molecule keeps one old strand. Copying doubles the DNA but not the chromosome count.

blocks.text: You found the partner of two strands base by base, and counted two molecules from one.
You also kept the chromosome count at 4 while the DNA doubled.

recap.nextHook: Copied chromosomes are ready to be shared out. How does a cell make two cells?

lessons.title: Make two cells

steps.headline: Mitosis shares a cell's copied chromosomes equally between two new nuclei.

lead.text: Before dividing, a cell copies its DNA. In mitosis the sister chromatids of every chromosome are pulled apart, and one copy goes to each new nucleus.
Cytokinesis then splits the cell. The results are two daughter cells.
Think of the worksheet. Each student got a full set. A daughter cell needs a full set of chromosomes too.

reveal.text: You predicted that each daughter keeps the parent's number. Sister chromatids separate equally, so the chromosome number does not change.

steps.headline: A cell has 3 chromosomes before replication. How many DNA molecules does it have afterwards?

workedSteps.text: Replication copies every chromosome. Each one now has two sister chromatids.
Each chromatid is one DNA molecule.
Count two molecules for each chromosome.

steps.headline: A cell has 6 chromosomes before replication. How many DNA molecules does it have afterwards?

workedSteps.text: Each chromosome is copied, so it has two chromatids.
Count two DNA molecules for each of the six chromosomes.

steps.headline: Cells divide when the body needs more of them. Division is regulated.

lead.text: Cells divide for growth, repair and reproduction. Signals and conditions switch division on and off, so a tissue makes only the cells it needs.
In an ideal case every cell divides once in each round, so every cell becomes two.

reveal.text: Three rounds gave three doublings. Real tissues grow more slowly, because only some cells divide in each round.

lead.text: In a real tissue, regulation decides which cells divide. Suppose that in one round, only half of the cells do.

reveal.text: Only the dividing cells added to the total, so the tissue grew by less than a doubling. That is regulation at work.

lessons.orientation: Track chromosomes through mitotic division and connect division to growth and repair.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A worksheet has 5 pages. A teacher photocopies the whole set once.
The original set goes to one student and the copy goes to another.

intro.promise: By the end you'll follow chromosomes through mitosis and count cells as a tissue grows.
intro.whyItMatters: It is how a single fertilised egg becomes a body, and how a cut heals.

recap.keyIdea: Mitosis copies the DNA and then shares it, so each daughter cell keeps the parent's chromosome number. Regulation decides which cells divide.

blocks.text: You followed 4 chromosomes into each daughter cell and counted DNA molecules after replication.
You also counted cells through ideal doublings and through a tissue where only some cells divide.

recap.nextHook: Sex cells need only half the chromosomes. How does a cell halve a chromosome set?

lessons.title: Halve a chromosome set

steps.headline: Body cells hold two sets of chromosomes. Gametes hold one.

lead.text: A diploid cell has two sets of chromosomes, one from each parent. Matching chromosomes from the two sets are homologous: they carry the same genes.
A gamete, such as an egg or a sperm, is haploid. It has one set.
At fertilisation, two gametes join. Think about what that does to the number of chromosome sets.

reveal.text: You added the two sets. Fertilisation brings two haploid sets together and restores the diploid number.

steps.headline: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes. Meiosis II separates sister chromatids.

lead.text: Meiosis copies the DNA once, then divides twice.
In the first division, homologous chromosomes are pulled apart. In the second, sister chromatids are pulled apart. The result is four haploid cells.

steps.headline: A cell has 3 homologous pairs. How many chromosomes does each cell have after both divisions?

workedSteps.text: Start diploid: three pairs.
Meiosis I sends one chromosome of each pair to each cell.
Meiosis II separates the sister chromatids. The count stays at 3 in each of four cells.

steps.headline: A starting cell has 4 chromosomes in 2 pairs. How many chromosomes does each final cell have?

workedSteps.text: Meiosis I sends one chromosome of each pair to each cell.
Meiosis II separates the sister chromatids. Count one chromosome from each pair.

lead.text: DNA is copied once at the start of meiosis. The cell then divides twice. Check what happens between the two divisions.

reveal.text: You counted no new copying. Two divisions share one round of copying, which is why the number halves.

lead.text: Two siblings have the same parents and the same chromosome count, yet they are not identical. Meiosis shuffles chromosomes, and chromosomes can swap segments.

reveal.text: Assortment and crossing over make every gamete different. The simple count diagram leaves crossing over out.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish homologues from sister chromatids and follow two meiotic divisions.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A human body cell has 46 chromosomes. An egg and a sperm join to make the first cell of a baby.
That first cell must have 46 chromosomes too.

intro.promise: By the end you'll follow chromosome numbers through the two divisions of meiosis and fertilisation.
intro.whyItMatters: It explains why each child is a mix of both parents.

recap.keyIdea: Meiosis copies the DNA once and divides twice, so gametes are haploid. Fertilisation restores diploid cells with a new mix of chromosomes.

blocks.text: You found that an egg carries 23 chromosomes and that a 3-pair cell gives gametes with 3. You also saw no copying between the divisions.
You explained why siblings differ.

recap.nextHook: Now follow a single gene through a cross. What could the offspring inherit?

lessons.title: What could the offspring inherit?

steps.headline: Each parent passes on one allele of a gene, chosen at random.

lead.text: A gene can come in different versions called alleles. A diploid organism has two alleles of each gene, one from each parent. That pair is its genotype.
A genotype with two different alleles, such as Aa, is heterozygous. Each gamete gets one of the two alleles, at random.

steps.headline: A Punnett square lists every way two gametes can pair.

lead.text: Write one parent's gametes along the top and the other parent's down the side. Each box is one pairing, and every box is equally likely.
To find a chance, count the boxes of one genotype and divide by the total.

steps.headline: Cross Aa with Aa. How many of the four boxes are Aa?

workedSteps.text: Each parent's gametes are A or a. Fill the boxes.
Two of the boxes show Aa.
Divide by the total number of boxes.

steps.headline: Cross Aa with Aa. What percentage of offspring is expected to be aa?

workedSteps.text: Fill the boxes.
Only one box is aa.

steps.headline: A dominant allele shows even when only one copy is present.

lead.text: The phenotype is the trait you can see. With complete dominance, one copy of the dominant allele, A, is enough to show it.
The recessive trait appears only when both alleles are recessive, as in aa.
Cross a heterozygous parent with a parent that has two recessive alleles. Fill the four boxes, then ask which of them show the recessive trait.

reveal.text: You counted the aa boxes. Only genotype aa shows the recessive trait, and this cross fills half its boxes with it.

lead.text: A family has four children from an Aa × Aa cross. The chance of aa for each child comes straight from the square.

reveal.text: The square gives the chance for each child. It does not set how many of a family's children will have aa.

lessons.orientation: Use a single-gene cross while separating genotype, phenotype and probability.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: You flip two fair coins, one after the other.
Each coin lands heads or tails with equal chance.

intro.promise: By the end you'll use a Punnett square to predict the chances of each genotype and trait in a single-gene cross.
intro.whyItMatters: It is how breeders and genetic counsellors estimate the chances of a trait.

recap.keyIdea: Each parent passes on one allele at random, and a Punnett square counts the equally likely pairings. The chances apply to each child.

blocks.text: You found that two coins give 25% for two heads, and that Aa × Aa gives 25% for aa and 50% for Aa.
You also saw that a family of four need not follow the percentages.

recap.nextHook: Now ask where a new allele comes from in the first place. Where does a new variant arise?

lessons.title: Where does a new variant come from?

steps.headline: A mutation is a change in the DNA sequence, and it arises by chance.

lead.text: A mutation is a change in the order of bases. A substitution swaps one base for another, so the length stays the same. Insertions and deletions add or remove bases.
Copying slips and damage cause mutations. They happen by chance.

steps.headline: Compare ACGT with AGGT. How many positions differ?

workedSteps.text: Align the sequences and compare each pair of letters.
One pair disagrees: C became G. The DNA has changed.
A changed base alone does not tell you what the change does. That needs evidence.

steps.headline: Compare AATG with AACG. How many positions differ?

workedSteps.text: Align the sequences and compare each pair of letters.
Count only the pairs that disagree.

steps.headline: Only a mutation in the cells that make gametes can pass to offspring.

lead.text: In a sexually reproducing animal, a mutation in the line of cells that makes eggs or sperm can reach the next generation.
A mutation in an ordinary body cell, such as a skin cell, generally stays in that body.
Real comparisons use longer sequences. Keep both in step and compare each pair of letters from the left.

reveal.text: You compared position by position. Each mismatch is one changed base, and the unchanged ones tell you what was copied faithfully.

steps.headline: Mutations are not made to order. Selection sorts the variants that already exist.

lead.text: Mutations arise by chance, whether or not they would help.
Whether a variant becomes common depends on whether it helps its carriers leave more offspring in their environment.
After an environmental change, one variant becomes more common in a population. Decide how that could happen without the organisms making it on purpose.

reveal.text: The variants already existed. Selection changed how common each one was, and it did not create the helpful one.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish DNA change from directed need and identify what can be inherited.
lessons.reviewLabel: Where does a new variant come from?
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A scribe copies a 500-word page by hand. On average, the scribe makes one slip in every 100 words.

intro.promise: By the end you'll spot a mutation by comparing sequences and say which mutations can be inherited and why they are not made on demand.
intro.whyItMatters: Mutations are the original source of all the variety that evolution sorts.

recap.keyIdea: A mutation is a chance change in DNA sequence, and only one in a gamete's line of cells can be inherited. Selection sorts variants and does not order them.

blocks.text: You spotted changed bases by comparing sequences position by position. You also traced which mutations reach children.

recap.nextHook: Now follow a variant through the generations. How does a population change over time?

lessons.title: A population changes over generations

steps.headline: A variant's frequency is its share of the whole population.

lead.text: Frequency is a variant's count divided by the whole population, usually written as a percentage.
A count and a frequency answer different questions. Doubling every count leaves every frequency unchanged.

steps.headline: Blue organisms increase from 10 of 40 to 20 of 40. By how many percentage points does the blue frequency rise?

workedSteps.text: Before: count divided by total.
Use frequencies, not counts, so that populations of any size compare fairly.
After: the same calculation.
Subtract the earlier frequency from the later one.

steps.headline: Blue organisms increase from 15 of 50 to 30 of 50. By how many points does the blue frequency rise?

workedSteps.text: Before: count divided by total.
After: the same calculation.
Subtract to find the rise.

steps.headline: Natural selection: heritable variants that leave more offspring become more common.

lead.text: The individuals in a population differ. Some differences are heritable: they pass from parents to offspring.
If carriers of one variant leave more offspring in their environment, that variant's frequency rises over the generations.
The same population can be placed in two environments. A variant that helps in one need not help in the other.

reveal.text: In environment B the green variant did worse, so its share fell. The same variant rose in environment A, and the environment decided which.

lead.text: You find that a variant has become more common in a small population. Before crediting selection, ask what else could change a frequency.

reveal.text: A frequency shift alone does not prove selection. Chance sampling, migration and other processes can also change a population's makeup.

lessons.orientation: Connect heritable variation and reproductive success without confusing change with proof of cause.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A meadow has 40 beetles: 16 green and 24 brown. Birds spot the green ones easily.
Before the beetles can breed, the birds eat half of the green beetles and none of the brown.

intro.promise: By the end you'll calculate how a variant's share of a population changes, and say what natural selection does and does not show.
intro.whyItMatters: It explains why populations fit their environments, from resistant bacteria to camouflaged insects.

recap.keyIdea: Heritable variants that leave more offspring become more common, and which variants do so depends on the environment. A frequency shift alone does not prove selection.

blocks.text: You turned counts into frequencies and measured rises of 25 and 30 percentage points. You also saw the same variant fall in a different environment.

recap.nextHook: Zoom out from one species to a whole habitat. Who eats whom?

lessons.title: Follow the food

steps.headline: In a food web, each arrow points from the food to the organism that eats it.

lead.text: A food web shows who eats whom. Algae → zooplankton means that zooplankton eat algae.
A producer, such as algae or grass, makes its own food. A consumer eats other organisms.

steps.headline: How many direct food sources does the heron have in this pond web?

workedSteps.text: Find the arrows that end at the heron.
Small fish → heron, and zooplankton → heron.
Follow each route back. Both start at algae.

steps.headline: How many direct food sources does the hawk have in this meadow web?

workedSteps.text: Find the arrows that end at the hawk.
Count only direct links.

steps.headline: Matter is recycled in an ecosystem. Energy flows through it and disperses.

lead.text: Decomposers return matter from dead material to the soil and water, where producers can use it again.
Energy is not recycled. Most of it disperses as heat, so an ecosystem needs a steady input, usually light.
Every route in a web starts somewhere. Look for the organism that does not need to eat anything.

reveal.text: You found the start of every route. Everything else in the pond depends on the algae, directly or through other consumers.

lead.text: A small web shows who eats whom. Imagine the number of mice falling and ask what you could say about the hawks.

reveal.text: Arrows show feeding links and say nothing about numbers. Predicting a count needs more than a small diagram.

lessons.orientation: Read feeding arrows and separate energy flow from recycled matter.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A pond has algae, tiny animals called zooplankton that eat the algae, and small fish that eat the zooplankton.
A disease kills most of the zooplankton.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read a food web's arrows and say which parts of an ecosystem are recycled and which are not.
intro.whyItMatters: It lets you predict what a change to one species does to the rest of a habitat.

recap.keyIdea: Arrows point from food to eater, and every route starts at a producer. Matter is recycled by decomposers, but energy flows through and disperses as heat.

blocks.text: You counted direct food sources for a heron and a hawk. You traced routes back to the producer and said why a diagram cannot predict a count.

recap.nextHook: Energy thins out along every route. How much reaches the top?

lessons.title: Why does less energy reach the top?

steps.headline: Only part of the energy at one trophic level reaches the next.

lead.text: A trophic level is a feeding step: producers, then the animals that eat them, then their predators.
Organisms use most of their energy to live, and not everything is eaten or digested. The percentage that passes up is the transfer efficiency.

steps.headline: Producers hold 4000 kJ. At 10% transfer, how much energy reaches level 3?

workedSteps.text: Level 2 receives a tenth of the producers' energy.
Level 3 receives a tenth of what level 2 holds.

steps.headline: Producers hold 2000 kJ. At 10% transfer, how much energy reaches level 3?

workedSteps.text: Level 2 receives a tenth of the producers' energy.
Level 3 receives a tenth of what level 2 holds.

steps.headline: 10% is a stated assumption, not a law of nature.

lead.text: Real transfer efficiencies differ between ecosystems, so problems state the figure to use.
A stated 20% passes twice as much energy as 10% from the same starting amount.
This problem states a different efficiency. Use the figure it gives, and apply it to the producers' energy.

reveal.text: You used the stated efficiency. The same method works for any figure, and a higher efficiency passes on more.

lead.text: Now the question runs the other way. The level below must hold more than the level above, by the factor the transfer takes away.

reveal.text: You worked backwards by dividing by the efficiency. Supporting a small amount at a high level takes a much larger amount lower down.

lessons.orientation: Calculate trophic transfers using an explicit efficiency assumption.
lessons.reviewLabel: Why does less energy reach the top?
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A farmer feeds a cow 100 kg of grain. Over the same time the cow gains 10 kg of body mass.

intro.promise: By the end you'll work out how much energy reaches each level of a food chain, forwards and backwards, from a stated efficiency.
intro.whyItMatters: It is why food chains are short and why meat needs far more land than plants.

recap.keyIdea: Only a stated fraction of energy passes to the next level, so energy shrinks at every step. Divide by the same fraction to work backwards.

blocks.text: You applied a 10% transfer once and twice, and tried a stated 20%. You also worked back from 300 kJ to 3000 kJ.

recap.nextHook: Populations grow until something stops them. Why can't a population grow forever?

lessons.title: Why can't a population grow forever?

steps.headline: With unlimited resources, a population grows by the same proportion each round.

lead.text: Under ideal conditions, a population grows by a constant proportion each round. Each round then adds more than the last.
Doubling is one example.
Compare the two curves: ideal doubling and growth in a real habitat. Think about what crowding does to food and space.

reveal.text: You predicted a slowdown. In the limited case the population still grows, but each round adds less than the one before.

steps.headline: A habitat can support only so many individuals. That limit is its carrying capacity.

lead.text: As numbers rise, food and space run short. Competition lowers births or raises deaths, and growth levels off near the carrying capacity.
Net growth is births minus deaths.

steps.headline: A closed population of 50 has 12 births and 7 deaths. What is its size afterwards?

workedSteps.text: A closed population gains only by births and loses only by deaths.
Net change is births minus deaths.
Add the net change to the starting size.

steps.headline: A closed population of 70 has 16 births and 9 deaths. What is its size afterwards?

workedSteps.text: Net change is births minus deaths.
Add the net change to the starting size.

lead.text: A population can hold a steady size for years. Count the gains and the losses over one interval.

reveal.text: Zero net change means gains and losses balance. It does not mean that every individual has stopped reproducing.

lead.text: A habitat's population was near its limit. Then a drought cuts the food supply.

reveal.text: Carrying capacity depends on conditions. A drought or habitat loss can lower it, so it is not a permanent constant for a species.

lessons.orientation: Compare proportional growth with resource-limited growth and changing carrying capacity.
lessons.reviewLabel: Why can't a population grow forever?
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A pond is 20 square metres. Water lilies cover 1 square metre of it today.
The patch doubles in area every day.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell unlimited growth from limited growth, and calculate how births and deaths change a population.
intro.whyItMatters: It explains why pest outbreaks, fish stocks and human populations rise, level off or crash.

recap.keyIdea: Unlimited growth gets faster each round, but limited resources slow it near the carrying capacity, which itself changes with conditions.

blocks.text: You doubled populations until they outgrew a pond, and calculated net change from births and deaths. You also saw a drought lower a habitat's limit.

recap.nextHook: Last, step back and ask how scientists know any of this. What would count as evidence?

lessons.title: What would count as evidence?

steps.headline: A fair test measures a defined outcome as change from the starting point.

lead.text: Decide the outcome before you measure, for example growth in height over three weeks.
Groups may start at different sizes, so compare each group's change from its baseline, which is its starting measurement.

steps.headline: Group A grows from 10 cm to 16 cm. Group B grows from 4 cm to 13 cm. Which group grew more?

workedSteps.text: Group A: final height minus baseline.
Group B: the same calculation.
Group B grew more, although group A ended taller.

steps.headline: Group A grows from 10 cm to 16 cm. How much did its mean height increase?

workedSteps.text: Use the group's own baseline.
Subtract the baseline from the final height.

steps.headline: Random assignment and independent replicates make a comparison fair.

lead.text: A control group gets no treatment. Comparable units are given the treatment by chance, which spreads other differences evenly between the groups.
Independent replicates, such as many separate pots, show how much results vary. Measuring one pot many times is not replication.
Compare the growth of the treated group with its matched control over the same interval.

reveal.text: You compared growth over the same interval. The difference between treated group and control is the treatment's apparent effect.

lead.text: Surveyors measure plants at many sites and find taller plants at the wetter ones. Nobody assigned the rainfall: this is an observation, not an experiment.

reveal.text: An association can suggest a hypothesis, but it does not isolate a cause. Other environmental factors may explain the pattern.

lessons.orientation: Design fair ecological comparisons and avoid turning correlation into an unsupported cause.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Plant A grows from 4 cm to 19 cm with fertiliser. Plant B grows from 12 cm to 22 cm without it.
Plant B ends up taller.

intro.promise: By the end you'll judge whether a plant experiment is fair, and say what an observed pattern can and cannot show.
intro.whyItMatters: It is how you can tell a real finding from a lucky or confused one.

recap.keyIdea: A fair ecological test compares matched groups by change from baseline, assigns treatments at random and replicates independently. An observed pattern alone does not show cause.

blocks.text: You compared growth instead of final height, and found that treated plants grew 3 cm more than their control. You also saw why a survey cannot isolate a cause.

recap.nextHook: That completes the course: from cells to ecosystems.

questions.prompt: Both cells need food in and waste out. Name the structure around each cell that controls this exchange.
hints: Look at the outline of each cell.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both cells exchange substances across a plasma membrane.

questions.onCorrect: The plasma membrane. Every cell has one, and it controls what enters and leaves.

misconceptions.feedback: A cell wall is an extra layer outside the boundary that some cells have. The boundary every cell has lies inside it.

questions.prompt: The bacterium has no membrane-bound nucleus. Where is its DNA?
hints: No nucleus does not mean no genetic material.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A bacterial nucleoid holds DNA without a surrounding nuclear membrane.

questions.onCorrect: In the nucleoid. A bacterium has DNA, but no membrane wraps it.

misconceptions.feedback: Every cell has DNA. The bacterium just keeps it without a nuclear membrane.
Chloroplasts capture light and are found in plant cells. Look for the region where bacterial DNA sits.

questions.prompt: Leaf cells capture light, but after dark they still need energy from fuel. Which organelle does that job?
hints: Which organelle transfers energy from fuel?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Leaf cells have chloroplasts for light and mitochondria for energy from fuel.

questions.onCorrect: Mitochondria. A leaf cell has both organelles because it does both jobs.

misconceptions.feedback: Chloroplasts need light. The job here goes on in the dark.

questions.prompt: Name the supporting structure outside the plant cell membrane.
hints: Look at the outermost layer of the leaf cell.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The cell wall gives external support; the membrane remains inside it.

questions.onCorrect: The cell wall. It props the cell up from outside and leaves the membrane in charge of exchange.

misconceptions.feedback: The membrane lies inside this layer. Name the structure outside it.

questions.prompt: A root cell is alive but has no chloroplasts. Which conclusion follows?
hints: Think about where roots are and what they do.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Many plant cells, including root cells, have no chloroplasts and use sugars made elsewhere.

choices.label: It cannot be a plant cell
It cannot release energy from fuel

questions.onCorrect: Not every plant cell photosynthesises. Root cells use sugars made by the leaves.

misconceptions.feedback: Plant cells are defined by more than chloroplasts. Roots are plant tissue.
Releasing energy from fuel is the mitochondria's job, and root cells have those.

questions.prompt: Name the structure whose presence most directly shows that a cell is eukaryotic.
hints: Pick the distinctive structure, not one every cell shares.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A membrane-bound nucleus distinguishes eukaryotic cells from bacterial cells.

questions.onCorrect: A nucleus. A plasma membrane is shared by all cells, so it can't tell the two types apart.

misconceptions.feedback: Bacteria have these too. Choose a structure bacteria lack.

questions.prompt: Equal volumes hold 12 solute units on the left and 4 on the right, and solute can cross. In which direction is there net movement at first?
hints: Which side is more concentrated? Compare amounts, since the volumes are equal.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The left side is more concentrated, so net solute movement is to the right.

questions.onCorrect: Left to right: from the more concentrated side to the less concentrated side.

misconceptions.feedback: That runs from the sparser side to the crowded one. Net movement goes the other way.
The two sides differ in concentration, so more particles cross one way than the other.

questions.prompt: Two fixed equal volumes contain 10 and 6 units of freely crossing solute. How many units are on each side at equilibrium?
hints: Keep the total solute constant.
Add the amounts on the two sides.
Divide the total between two equal volumes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The 16 units divide equally: 16 ÷ 2 = 8.

questions.onCorrect: 8 each. Total solute stays constant, and equal volumes finish with equal amounts.

misconceptions.feedback: That's both sides together. Share it between the two compartments.
That's the left side's starting amount. Some of it has moved across.

questions.prompt: 12 solute units start on the left and 4 on the right. The barrier blocks both solute and water. How many solute units are on the left after a long time?
hints: Check what can cross first.
If nothing can cross, can any amount change?
Each side keeps the amount it started with.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Nothing can cross, so each side keeps its starting amount: 12 on the left.

questions.onCorrect: 12. A barrier that blocks the solute leaves the amounts unchanged, whatever the difference in concentration.

misconceptions.feedback: That would need solute to cross, and this barrier blocks it.
That's the right side's amount. Ask about the left side.

questions.prompt: At equal concentration, 8 units are on each side. How many solute units are in the whole two-compartment system?
hints: Count both compartments.
There are eight units in each.
Add the two equal amounts.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 8 + 8 = 16 units. Diffusion does not destroy solute.

questions.onCorrect: 16. Equilibrium means equal concentrations, not missing solute: the total is unchanged.

misconceptions.feedback: That's one side. Count both compartments.

questions.prompt: At diffusion equilibrium, which statement is accurate?
hints: Separate no net change from no motion.

acceptedIdeas: Molecules cross both ways with no net flow
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Equilibrium is dynamic: opposite flows balance on average.

choices.label: Molecules cross both ways with no net flow
All molecules move in one direction

questions.onCorrect: Particles keep crossing both ways at equal rates, so there is no net flow.

misconceptions.feedback: Particles keep moving. What stops is the net change in concentration.
One-way movement would keep changing the concentrations. At equilibrium the flows balance.

questions.prompt: A separate equal-volume system starts with 14 solute units on one side and 2 on the other. How many units must move net from the concentrated side to reach equilibrium?
hints: Find the equilibrium amount first.
The total is shared between two equal volumes.
Subtract the equilibrium amount from the starting amount on the crowded side.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each side finishes with 8. The concentrated side loses 14 − 8 = 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Find the equal share first, then see how far the crowded side must fall to reach it.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the amount each side ends with. How many had to move to get there?
That's the gap between the sides. Only half of the gap has to cross.

questions.prompt: Water can cross but solute cannot. Equal volumes hold 4 solute units on the left and 12 on the right, at equal pressure. Which side gains water at first?
hints: Compare the concentrations, then follow the water.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The right side is more concentrated in solute, so it initially gains water.

questions.onCorrect: The right side, where the solute is more concentrated. Water moves toward more solute.

misconceptions.feedback: The left side has less solute. Water moves toward the more concentrated side, not away from it.

questions.prompt: As water enters the right compartment, what happens to its 12 solute units?
hints: The membrane's selectivity stays the same.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The membrane blocks solute; only its concentration changes.

questions.onCorrect: They stay. Only the water moves, so the solute is simply spread through a bigger volume.

misconceptions.feedback: Solute is never destroyed. It stays where it is.
The membrane blocks the solute, so it cannot cross.

questions.prompt: A compartment contains 12 solute units in volume 2. What is its concentration in units per volume?
hints: Use amount divided by volume.
Identify the amount and the volume in the question.
Divide the amount by the volume.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Concentration = 12 ÷ 2 = 6 units per volume.

questions.onCorrect: 6 per volume. Concentration is the amount of solute divided by the volume.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the amount by the volume. Concentration divides.
That's the amount alone. Divide by the volume.

questions.prompt: Why can the two volumes change while the total solute stays constant?
hints: Follow each substance separately.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Changing the water distribution changes volumes without changing solute amount.

questions.onCorrect: Water moves and solute stays, so volumes change but each side's solute amount does not.

misconceptions.feedback: Solute stays solute. Only the water moves across.
Nothing creates solute here. Its amount is fixed on each side.

questions.prompt: A compartment contains 8 units of trapped solute. Its volume increases from 1 to 2. By what factor is its concentration multiplied?
hints: Calculate the concentration before and after.
The solute amount is unchanged.
Divide the new concentration by the old one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Concentration changes from 8 to 4, a factor of 4 ÷ 8 = 0.5.

questions.onCorrect: 0.5. Doubling the volume halves the concentration when the solute amount is fixed.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be a doubling. The volume grew, so the concentration fell.
That's the new concentration, not the factor between old and new.

questions.prompt: A plant cell wall builds an opposing pressure as water enters. Which prediction is justified?
hints: The real cell includes a force that the model leaves out.

acceptedIdeas: Pressure can reduce or stop net water entry
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Water movement depends on both solute concentration and pressure; the simple partition model omits this opposition.

choices.label: Water must keep entering without limit
Pressure can reduce or stop net water entry

questions.onCorrect: Pressure can reduce or stop net entry. Water movement depends on pressure as well as solute.

misconceptions.feedback: That ignores the wall. As the cell swells, the wall pushes back.
Nothing in the wall's pushing damages the membrane. The pressure just opposes more water entering.

questions.prompt: Name the energy barrier that an enzyme lowers.
hints: The barrier must be crossed for a reaction to proceed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An enzyme provides a reaction pathway with lower activation energy.

questions.onCorrect: Activation energy. A lower barrier means more reactions get over it each second.

misconceptions.feedback: That is not the barrier. Name the energy a reaction needs before it can start.

questions.prompt: Enzyme A's rates at 10, 25, 40 and 55°C are 2, 8, 12 and 3 units per minute. What is the highest rate measured, in units per minute?
hints: Compare all four measured rates.
Pick the largest of the four.
Use the plotted value, not a guess about other temperatures.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The largest of 2, 8, 12 and 3 is 12 units per minute, at 40°C.

questions.onCorrect: 12 units per minute, at 40°C. This is the best of the temperatures that were tested.

misconceptions.feedback: 40 is the temperature. The question asks for the rate.
That is the lowest rate, at the highest temperature.

questions.prompt: Once many active sites are occupied, which substance limits the maximum rate in this example?
hints: Ask which component supplies the active sites.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The fixed amount of enzyme limits how many substrate molecules can be processed at once.

questions.onCorrect: The enzyme. With every active site busy, extra substrate can't be processed any faster.

misconceptions.feedback: There is plenty of substrate. What is short is the thing that processes it.

questions.prompt: After 3 minutes, the matched enzyme sample has 27 product units and the control has 9. What is the difference?
hints: Compare the same elapsed time.
Read both amounts at three minutes.
Subtract the control from the enzyme sample.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 27 − 9 = 18 extra product units in this comparison.

questions.onCorrect: 18 extra units. A matched control lets you credit that difference to the enzyme.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two samples. A comparison subtracts.
That's the enzyme sample alone. Compare it with the control.

questions.prompt: A high-temperature treatment lowers one enzyme's activity. What is a plausible explanation?
hints: A protein's shape matters to its function.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: High temperature can denature an enzyme and disrupt binding or catalysis.

choices.label: Every enzyme works best at that temperature

questions.onCorrect: Its shape changed. A denatured active site no longer fits the substrate.

misconceptions.feedback: The activity fell, so this temperature is not the best one for this enzyme.
Past a point heat damages enzymes. Here the activity went down.

questions.prompt: Which experiment best tests an enzyme's effect?
hints: Separate the tested factor from other possible causes.

acceptedIdeas: Compare matched replicated samples that differ only in enzyme addition
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Holding other conditions constant isolates enzyme addition, while replication estimates variability.

choices.label: Change enzyme, temperature and pH together
Compare different organisms at unrelated times
Compare matched replicated samples that differ only in enzyme addition

questions.onCorrect: Change one thing and keep the rest matched, with repeats. Any difference then points to the enzyme.

misconceptions.feedback: With three changes at once, you can't tell which one caused the difference.
Different organisms and times add many other differences.

questions.prompt: Name the gas that supplies the carbon atoms in a leaf's newly made sugar.
hints: Trace atoms separately from energy.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Carbon dioxide supplies the carbon atoms; light supplies energy.

questions.onCorrect: Carbon dioxide. Light brings energy; the atoms for the sugar come from the gas.

misconceptions.feedback: Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis. Look for the gas that contains carbon.
Light is energy. It has no atoms to give.

questions.prompt: One glucose has six carbon atoms. Each CO₂ supplies one. How many CO₂ molecules supply the carbon for two glucose molecules?
hints: Count the carbon atoms in both glucose molecules.
Each glucose has six carbon atoms.
Each CO₂ contributes one carbon atom.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two glucose contain 2 × 6 = 12 carbon atoms, so they need 12 CO₂.

questions.onCorrect: 12. Count the carbon atoms in the sugar, because each came from one CO₂.

misconceptions.feedback: That is enough for one glucose. There are two.
That counts the glucose molecules. Count the carbon atoms.

questions.prompt: In photosynthesis, in what form is light energy stored?
hints: Think of the sugar the plant makes.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Photosynthesis captures some incoming light energy as chemical energy in sugar.

questions.onCorrect: Chemical energy, held in the bonds of sugar. Light itself adds no matter.

misconceptions.feedback: Some energy is lost as heat, but the energy that is captured is stored differently.
Carbon is matter. The question asks about the form of the energy.

questions.prompt: With a low supply of CO₂, the photosynthetic rate is 8 at light level 60 and 8 at light level 80. By how much did the rate increase?
hints: Use the two rates given for the lower curve.
Subtract the first rate from the second.
What is the difference between two equal rates?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 8 − 8 = 0. The curve is flat between those light levels.

questions.onCorrect: Zero. The curve has plateaued, so something else, here the CO₂ supply, is limiting the rate.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the rate itself, not the change in it.
That is the change in light level, not in the rate.

questions.prompt: A leaf cell has chloroplasts. Name the process, besides photosynthesis, that it uses to transfer energy from sugar.
hints: Photosynthesis does not replace every other cell process.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Leaf cells also respire to support their energy needs.

questions.onCorrect: Respiration. Photosynthesis stores the energy, and respiration releases it for the cell's work.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the process the question rules out. Name the other one.

questions.prompt: Using the simplified overall equation, how many O₂ molecules accompany the formation of three glucose molecules?
hints: Read the number written in front of O₂.
Use that number of oxygen molecules for each glucose.
Multiply by three glucose molecules.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each glucose corresponds to six O₂: 3 × 6 = 18.

questions.onCorrect: 18. Six O₂ come with each glucose, so scale by the number of glucose molecules.

misconceptions.feedback: That is for one glucose. There are three.
That counts the glucose molecules. Multiply by the oxygen made for each one.

questions.prompt: Name the molecule that commonly transfers energy from respiration to cellular work.
hints: The name is three letters long.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ATP couples energy-releasing processes to energy-requiring work.

questions.onCorrect: ATP. Cells fill it with energy from fuel, then spend it on work.

misconceptions.feedback: Glucose is the fuel. Name the molecule that carries the transferred energy to the work.

questions.prompt: Complete aerobic oxidation of two glucose molecules produces how many CO₂ molecules?
hints: Each CO₂ contains one carbon.
Each glucose contains six carbons.
Count the carbon from two glucose molecules.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each glucose contributes six carbon atoms: 2 × 6 = 12 CO₂.

questions.onCorrect: 12. Each carbon atom from the fuel ends up in one CO₂.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the CO₂ from one glucose. There are two.
That counts the glucose molecules. Count the carbon atoms in them.

questions.prompt: A living plant has stored fuel and oxygen but no light. Name the energy-transfer process that can continue.
hints: Which process uses fuel rather than incoming light?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Respiration can use stored fuel in darkness even when photosynthesis stops.

questions.onCorrect: Respiration. It runs on stored fuel, so it carries on when the light goes.

misconceptions.feedback: Photosynthesis needs light, and there is none. Name the process that uses fuel.

questions.prompt: A sealed jar of living organisms holds 20 units of oxygen at the start and 11 units after three minutes. How many units were consumed?
hints: Compare the starting and final oxygen amounts.
The final amount is lower.
Subtract the final amount from the starting amount.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 20 − 11 = 9 oxygen units.

questions.onCorrect: 9 units. Falling oxygen in a sealed jar is a sign that organisms are respiring.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what was left. The question asks how much was used.
That adds the two amounts. Oxygen fell, so subtract.

questions.prompt: What happens to glucose's carbon during complete aerobic oxidation?
hints: Follow the carbon-containing substances.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Glucose carbon is conserved in CO₂; energy transfer does not destroy those atoms.

questions.onCorrect: It ends up in carbon dioxide. Atoms are conserved, and only the energy is transferred.

misconceptions.feedback: Matter doesn't turn into energy. The carbon atoms are still there afterwards.
Oxygen gas has no carbon in it. Look for a product that does.

questions.prompt: Which claim correctly separates breathing from cellular respiration?
hints: Compare moving air with cellular chemistry.

acceptedIdeas: Breathing moves air; cellular respiration transfers energy through chemical reactions
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Breathing can supply oxygen, but respiration is a set of chemical processes in cells.

choices.label: They are exactly the same reaction
Breathing moves air; cellular respiration transfers energy through chemical reactions

questions.onCorrect: Breathing moves air. Respiration is the chemistry that goes on in cells.

misconceptions.feedback: Breathing is a movement of air, not a reaction. Respiration is the reaction.
Plants and bacteria respire too, and they do not breathe.

questions.prompt: A new DNA base is placed opposite adenine (A). Give the name of its complementary base.
hints: The letters pair A with T, and C with G.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Adenine pairs with thymine in standard DNA base pairing.

questions.onCorrect: Thymine. A pairs with T, so the old strand decides which base comes next.

misconceptions.feedback: Those bases pair with each other, not with adenine.
Uracil is found in RNA. In DNA, adenine pairs with a different base.

questions.prompt: Write the partner bases beneath the strand 5′-AAGC-3′, from left to right.
hints: Pair one position at a time, keeping the same left-to-right order.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The aligned partner is 3′-TTCG-5′; the two strands run in opposite directions.

questions.onCorrect: TTCG. Each base takes its partner in turn, and the partner strand runs the opposite way.

misconceptions.feedback: That reverses the order. Keep the partner bases in step with the strand above.
That copies the strand itself. Write each base's partner.

questions.prompt: A double-stranded DNA molecule replicates once. How many double-stranded DNA molecules result?
hints: Separate strands serve as templates.
Each old strand receives a new partner.
Count the resulting paired molecules.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One molecule is copied into two, each with one old and one new strand.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Each old strand gets a new partner, so one molecule gives two.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts strands. The question asks for double-stranded molecules.
The old strands each get a partner, which makes more than one molecule.

questions.prompt: A cell has 4 chromosomes before copying. Immediately after copying, while sister chromatids remain joined, how many chromosomes does it have?
hints: DNA amount and chromosome number are different counts.
Joined sister chromatids belong to one replicated chromosome.
Keep the chromosome count unchanged at this stage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: It still has four chromosomes; each now has two sister chromatids.

questions.onCorrect: 4. Copying doubles the DNA but not the number of chromosomes.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the chromatids. Joined chromatids still make one chromosome each.
Copying does not halve anything. The count stays as it was.

questions.prompt: What does semiconservative replication keep in each resulting DNA molecule?
hints: Trace the two original strands separately.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each resulting molecule pairs an original template strand with a newly made strand.

questions.onCorrect: One original strand, paired with a new one. Each molecule is half old and half new.

misconceptions.feedback: The two original strands separate. Each ends up in a different molecule.
Every old strand is reused as a template, so each new molecule contains one.

questions.prompt: Six chromosomes each have two sister chromatids after copying. How many DNA molecules are present?
hints: Count both chromatids of each chromosome.
There are six replicated chromosomes.
Multiply the chromosomes by the chromatids in each.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each chromatid contains one DNA molecule: 6 × 2 = 12.

questions.onCorrect: 12. Each chromatid is one DNA molecule, and every chromosome now has two.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts chromosomes. Each one now holds two DNA molecules.
That is the chromatids in one chromosome. There are more chromosomes.

questions.prompt: Name the nuclear division process used in ordinary tissue growth and repair.
hints: It keeps the starting chromosome number.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Mitosis distributes copied chromosomes to daughter nuclei during regulated growth and repair.

questions.onCorrect: Mitosis. It shares copied chromosomes so each daughter nucleus gets a full set.

misconceptions.feedback: Meiosis makes sex cells and halves the chromosome number. Growth needs the full number kept.

questions.prompt: A cell has 6 chromosomes before replication. How many DNA molecules does it have after replication but before mitosis?
hints: Replication copies the DNA.
Each of the six chromosomes now has two chromatids.
Count the two DNA molecules in every replicated chromosome.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Six replicated chromosomes have two chromatids each: 12 DNA molecules.

questions.onCorrect: 12. Every chromosome is copied, so it holds two DNA molecules.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of chromosomes. Each one now holds two DNA molecules.
That doubles twice. Replication copies each chromosome only once.

questions.prompt: A cell starts with 4 chromosomes and completes normal mitosis and cytokinesis. How many chromosomes are in each daughter cell?
hints: Think about the worksheet: each student got a full set.
Sister chromatids are separated equally.
Each daughter gets the same number the parent started with.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each daughter retains the original four chromosomes.

questions.onCorrect: 4. Mitosis gives each daughter a full set, so the chromosome number stays the same.

misconceptions.feedback: Mitosis does not halve the number. Each daughter gets a full set.
That counts the chromatids before they separate. Each daughter gets one copy of each chromosome.

questions.prompt: One cell completes three ideal rounds of division, with every descendant dividing each round. How many cells result?
hints: Double once for each round.
After two rounds there are four cells.
Double the count a third time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sequence is 1 → 2 → 4 → 8.

questions.onCorrect: 8. Each round doubles the number of cells, so three rounds make three doublings.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds two for each round. Each round doubles the count instead.
That counts the rounds. The question asks for the number of cells.

questions.prompt: Name the two joined copies of a replicated chromosome that separate during mitosis.
hints: Track the two copies made by DNA replication.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sister chromatids separate and become daughter chromosomes.

questions.onCorrect: Sister chromatids. They separate so each daughter nucleus gets one copy.

misconceptions.feedback: Homologous chromosomes are separate chromosomes from two parents. The joined copies came from one.

questions.prompt: Does a normal body cell divide only because it is about to die?
hints: Separate regulated division from cell death.

acceptedIdeas: No, division is regulated for growth, repair and other needs
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Cell-cycle regulation responds to conditions and signals; imminent death is not the general cause.

choices.label: Yes, that is the defining trigger
No, division is regulated for growth, repair and other needs
Yes, and the DNA need not be copied

questions.onCorrect: No. Division is regulated and happens when the body needs new cells.

misconceptions.feedback: Cells divide when growth or repair needs them to. Dying is not the trigger.
DNA is always copied first. Without a copy, a daughter would lack half its instructions.

questions.prompt: A diploid cell has 3 homologous pairs. How many chromosomes does it contain before DNA replication?
hints: Each pair contains two homologues.
There are three pairs.
Multiply the pairs by the chromosomes in each.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three pairs contain 3 × 2 = 6 chromosomes.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Each homologous pair holds two chromosomes, so count them in twos.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of pairs. Each pair holds two chromosomes.
Replication has not happened yet, so nothing has been doubled.

questions.prompt: Meiosis I separates one kind of chromosome relationship. Name the paired chromosomes it pulls apart.
hints: The pair holds matching chromosomes from the two sets.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Homologous chromosomes separate first; sister chromatids remain joined.

questions.onCorrect: Homologous chromosomes. Pulling them apart is what halves the chromosome number.

misconceptions.feedback: Sister chromatids stay joined in meiosis I. They part in the second division.

questions.prompt: A starting cell has 4 chromosomes in 2 pairs. After the two meiotic divisions, how many chromosomes does each final cell have?
hints: Meiosis reduces two chromosome sets to one.
The starting cell has two homologous pairs.
Take one chromosome from each pair.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each final haploid cell has one from each pair: two chromosomes.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Each final cell holds one chromosome from each pair.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the starting number. Each final cell has only one set.
A final cell has one from each pair, and there are two pairs.

questions.prompt: Two gametes each contain 3 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in their diploid fertilisation product?
hints: Fertilisation combines the two sets.
Each gamete supplies three chromosomes.
Add the two contributions.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 3 + 3 = 6 chromosomes.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Two haploid sets combine to restore a diploid cell.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one gamete's contribution. Fertilisation brings two together.
Each gamete supplies three, so add only those two amounts.

questions.prompt: How many additional DNA-replication rounds normally occur between meiosis I and meiosis II?
hints: Trace the copied chromosomes through both divisions.
Meiosis begins with one replication round.
Between the divisions, the DNA is divided again without being recopied.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: No additional replication occurs; the second division separates existing sister chromatids.

questions.onCorrect: Zero. The second division separates the copies already made, so the amount of DNA halves again.

misconceptions.feedback: That round happens once, before meiosis I. None happens between the divisions.
Each division is a separation, not a copying.

questions.prompt: Why can siblings inherit different chromosome combinations?
hints: Chromosome counts can match while the combinations differ.

acceptedIdeas: Chromosomes assort and exchange segments during meiosis
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Assortment and crossing over produce varied gametes; the simple count diagram omits crossover.

choices.label: Each parent has no genetic variation
Chromosomes assort and exchange segments during meiosis

questions.onCorrect: Chromosomes assort and swap segments, so every gamete carries a different mix.

misconceptions.feedback: Parents carry different versions of genes on their chromosomes.
Gametes differ from one another because of how meiosis shuffles chromosomes.

questions.prompt: What term describes the Aa parent, which carries two different alleles at this gene?
hints: The term contrasts with homozygous.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Aa is heterozygous; its two different alleles can separate into gametes.

questions.onCorrect: Heterozygous. Two different alleles, so it can pass on either one.

misconceptions.feedback: Homozygous means both alleles are the same. Aa has two different ones.

questions.prompt: For Aa × Aa, what percentage of offspring is expected to have genotype aa?
hints: Look at all four pairings.
Count the aa boxes.
Convert the fraction of boxes to a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One of four equally likely pairings is aa: 1 ÷ 4 = 25%.

questions.onCorrect: 25%. One box in four is aa, and each box is equally likely.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance of Aa. aa fills only one box.
That is the chance of the dominant phenotype. The question asks about genotype aa.

questions.prompt: With A completely dominant, which genotypes have the dominant phenotype?
hints: Keep genotype letters separate from the expressed trait.

acceptedIdeas: Two dominant alleles, or one of each
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One A allele is enough for the dominant phenotype in this model.

choices.label: Two dominant alleles, or one of each

questions.onCorrect: AA and Aa both. One dominant allele is enough to show the dominant trait.

misconceptions.feedback: Two recessive alleles give the recessive trait. Look for the genotypes that hide it.
Every organism has two alleles at the gene, so one of the options must apply.

questions.prompt: Four offspring are produced from Aa × Aa. Which statement is justified?
hints: A probability describes the long-run pattern.

acceptedIdeas: Each has a 25% chance of being aa
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Independent random outcomes do not enforce a fixed family quota.

choices.label: Each has a 25% chance of being aa

questions.onCorrect: Each offspring has the same chance. Four children need not include exactly one aa.

misconceptions.feedback: Each birth is independent. A family can have none, or several.
A quarter of pairings are aa, so each child has a chance of it.

questions.prompt: For Aa × aa, what percentage of offspring is expected to show the recessive phenotype?
hints: The aa parent always passes on a.
The Aa parent passes on a half the time.
Convert that fraction to a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two of four equally likely pairings are aa: 2 ÷ 4 = 50%.

questions.onCorrect: 50%. Only aa shows the recessive trait, and half the offspring are aa.

misconceptions.feedback: The Aa parent passes on A half the time, and those offspring show the dominant trait.
That is the chance for Aa × Aa. This cross has an aa parent, which changes the odds.

questions.prompt: In this model, Aa and AA share a phenotype. What term describes A relative to a?
hints: Name how the allele is expressed, not how common it is.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A is dominant in this genotype-to-phenotype relationship; that does not establish its frequency or fitness effect.

questions.onCorrect: Dominant. It shows whenever it is present, but that says nothing about how common it is.

misconceptions.feedback: The recessive allele is the one that shows only with two copies. A shows with one.
Dominance is about expression. It does not mean the allele is common.

questions.prompt: ATCG changes to ATGG without changing length. Name this type of single-base change.
hints: No base was inserted or removed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The third base was substituted: C became G.

questions.onCorrect: A substitution. One base was swapped for another, so the length stayed the same.

misconceptions.feedback: An insertion or deletion would change the length. Here the length stayed the same.

questions.prompt: Compare AATG with AACG. How many displayed positions differ?
hints: Align the sequences from the left.
Compare each pair of letters in turn.
Count the mismatches.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only position three differs: T became C.

questions.onCorrect: 1. Compare position by position and count only the mismatches.

misconceptions.feedback: The sequences are not identical. Check each pair of letters.
