Only one pair of letters disagrees. Check each pair again.

questions.prompt: Name the reproductive cell type that can carry a DNA mutation directly into an offspring at fertilisation.
hints: Ordinary skin cells do not contribute DNA at fertilisation.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A contributing gamete can carry a DNA variant into the offspring.

questions.onCorrect: A gamete. Only the egg and sperm pass DNA to the next generation.

misconceptions.feedback: Body cells do not take part in fertilisation. Name the cell that does.

questions.prompt: A useful variant becomes more frequent after an environmental change. Which explanation avoids a directed-mutation error?
hints: Separate where a variant comes from from how it spreads.

acceptedIdeas: Existing heritable variants differed in reproductive success
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Selection can change the frequency of existing variants; need does not direct a specific helpful mutation.

choices.label: Organisms created exactly the mutation they needed
Existing heritable variants differed in reproductive success
Every individual rewrote its DNA on purpose

questions.onCorrect: Variants were already there. Those that helped their carriers leave more offspring became more common.

misconceptions.feedback: Mutations are not made to order. The variant was already present or arose by chance.
Individuals cannot rewrite their DNA to meet a need.

questions.prompt: What can you conclude from a single DNA substitution alone?
hints: A changed letter does not specify a phenotype.

acceptedIdeas: Its biological effect needs additional evidence
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Effects depend on sequence context and environment; some substitutions have little detectable effect.

choices.label: Its biological effect needs additional evidence

questions.prompt: Compare the aligned sequences TCGATA and TCAACA. How many positions differ?
hints: Keep both sequences aligned.
Check each of the six positions in turn.
Count the mismatched pairs only.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Positions 3 and 5 differ; the other four agree.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Positions 3 and 5 disagree, so two bases have changed.

misconceptions.feedback: There is another mismatch. Check every position.
That is the length of the sequences. Count only the positions that differ.

questions.prompt: 10 of 40 organisms carry the blue variant. What percentage is blue?
hints: Use the blue count divided by the total.
The total is the blue and the other colour together.
Convert the fraction to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: 25%. A frequency is the variant's count divided by the whole population.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count. Divide it by the whole population and convert to a percentage.
That is the share that is not blue.

questions.prompt: Heritable variants consistently leave different numbers of reproducing descendants. Name the evolutionary process described.
hints: The difference is consistent, unlike random sampling.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Natural selection changes frequencies through differences in reproductive success associated with heritable traits.

questions.onCorrect: Natural selection. Heritable differences in offspring numbers shift the frequencies.

misconceptions.feedback: Mutation creates new variants. This is the sorting of variants that already exist.
The question says the difference is consistent and tied to the variant, which is not chance.

questions.prompt: Blue organisms increase from 15 of 50 to 30 of 50. By how many percentage points does the blue frequency rise?
hints: Calculate each frequency using the total of 50.
Convert each fraction to a percentage.
Subtract the earlier percentage from the later one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The frequency rises from 30% to 60%, a 30-point increase.

questions.onCorrect: 30 points. Work out both frequencies, then subtract.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the rise in count. The question asks for the rise in frequency.
That is the later frequency, not the rise.

questions.prompt: A small population's variant frequency changes. Is selection the only possible cause?
hints: A pattern can have more than one cause.

acceptedIdeas: No, chance and migration can also matter
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Several evolutionary processes can change frequency; causal evidence is needed.

choices.label: Yes, every frequency shift proves selection
No, chance and migration can also matter

questions.onCorrect: No. Chance and migration also shift frequencies, so a shift alone does not show selection.

misconceptions.feedback: A shift only shows that a frequency changed. It does not say why.
Populations change all the time, which is why the question matters.

questions.prompt: A once-useful trait becomes disadvantageous after a habitat change. Is this compatible with natural selection?
hints: Fitness depends on context.

acceptedIdeas: Yes, reproductive advantage depends on the environment
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Selection depends on how traits affect reproduction in the current environment.

choices.label: No, useful traits are always useful
Only if the organism chooses it
Yes, reproductive advantage depends on the environment

questions.onCorrect: Yes. A trait's advantage depends on the environment, so a new habitat can reverse it.

misconceptions.feedback: Usefulness depends on the environment, so a trait can stop helping.
Organisms do not choose the effect of their traits. The environment sets it.

questions.prompt: A later population has 18 blue and 42 gold organisms. What percentage is blue?
hints: Find the total population.
Divide the blue count by the total.
Convert the result to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: 30%. Blue is 18 of 60, so its share is a little under a third.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the blue count. Divide it by the whole population.
That is the share that is gold.

questions.prompt: What does the arrow Grass → Grasshopper mean?
hints: Follow the direction of matter and energy transfer.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Arrows run from food to consumer.

choices.label: Grass turns directly into a hawk

questions.onCorrect: The grasshopper eats the grass. An arrow runs from the food to the eater.

misconceptions.feedback: That reads the arrow backwards. It points to whichever organism is doing the eating.
An arrow shows eating, not turning into another organism.

questions.prompt: A pond web has algae, zooplankton, small fish and a heron. Which of these is the producer?
hints: Which organism makes its own food from light?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Algae build organic matter using light; the other organisms consume other organisms.

questions.onCorrect: Algae. They build their own food, so all the other organisms depend on them.

misconceptions.feedback: Animals eat other organisms. The producer is the one that makes its own food.

questions.prompt: In a meadow web, a hawk eats mice and frogs. Frogs eat grasshoppers, which eat grass. How many direct food sources does the hawk have?
hints: Count the arrows ending at the hawk.
Do not count indirect food sources.
Ignore the grass and the grasshopper: the hawk does not eat them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two arrows enter the hawk: one from mouse and one from frog.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Count only the arrows that end at the hawk.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every organism in the web. Count only those the hawk eats directly.
That includes organisms further down the routes. Count only direct links.

questions.prompt: Energy flows through ecosystems and becomes less available for further biological work. In what form does much of it disperse?
hints: Think about metabolic energy that is not passed into new biomass.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Energy disperses as heat; atoms can be recycled through environmental pools.

questions.onCorrect: Heat. Energy flows through and spreads out as heat, so ecosystems need a steady input.

misconceptions.feedback: Atoms are recycled. Energy is not, and it spreads out in another form.

questions.prompt: The number of mice decreases. Can a small food web diagram give an exact future hawk count?
hints: Check what the arrows actually show.

acceptedIdeas: No, other food sources and conditions also matter
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A feeding web shows relationships, not a complete quantitative population model.

choices.label: Yes, arrows specify exact population changes
No, other food sources and conditions also matter

questions.onCorrect: No. Arrows show who eats whom, not how many. Other food and conditions matter too.

misconceptions.feedback: Arrows show feeding links only. They give no numbers.
The hawk also eats frogs, so losing mice does not remove its food entirely.

questions.prompt: A pond web is a chain of algae, zooplankton, small fish and a heron, plus one extra link where the heron also eats zooplankton directly. How many feeding links does the web have in total?
hints: Count the links in the chain first.
A chain of four organisms has one fewer link than organisms.
Add the extra link.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The chain has 3 links, and the extra link makes 4.

questions.onCorrect: 4. Count the links in the chain, then add the shortcut.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chain alone. Add the extra link.
That is one more than the web has. A chain of four organisms has three links.

questions.prompt: Producers contain 1000 kJ of energy in the stated accounting. At an assumed 10% transfer, how many kJ reach the next level?
hints: Convert the percentage to a decimal fraction.
Apply the fraction to the producers' energy.
Multiply the producers' energy by one tenth.
questions.onCorrect: 100 kJ. A 10% transfer passes on one tenth of the energy.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the energy that does not pass on. The question asks how much reaches the next level.
That multiplies by ten. A percentage below a hundred makes the amount smaller.

questions.prompt: Starting with 2000 kJ, how many kJ reach level 3 after two assumed 10% transfers?
hints: Level 3 is two steps above the producers.
Apply 10% at each step.
Take one tenth of the energy left after the first step.
questions.onCorrect: 20 kJ. Two 10% steps leave 1% of the starting energy.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the energy at level 2. One more transfer is needed to reach level 3.
That subtracts a tenth instead of passing on a tenth.

questions.prompt: With 5000 kJ at producers and a 20% transfer at each step, how many kJ reach level 2?
hints: Use the stated efficiency.
A fifth is the same as 20%.
Take one fifth of the producers' energy.
questions.onCorrect: 1000 kJ. A stated 20% passes on twice as much as 10% would from the same start.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 10% of the producers' energy. This problem states 20%.
That is the energy that does not pass on. Level 2 receives the share that does.

questions.prompt: A next level needs 300 kJ at an assumed 10% transfer. How many kJ are required in the level below?
hints: Work backward through the transfer.
The required output is one tenth of the input.
Divide the required energy by the efficiency as a decimal.
questions.onCorrect: 3000 kJ. Working backwards means dividing by the efficiency.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the efficiency, which goes forwards. Work backwards by dividing.
That adds a tenth back on. Divide by the efficiency to undo it.

questions.prompt: Does every real food web transfer exactly 10% between levels?
hints: Separate a modelling assumption from a measured law.

acceptedIdeas: No, efficiency varies and must be specified or measured
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The ten-percent value is a useful stated approximation, not an exact universal constant.

choices.label: No, efficiency varies and must be specified or measured
No, energy is always fully transferred

questions.onCorrect: No. Efficiency varies between systems, so a problem states the value to use.

misconceptions.feedback: Measured efficiencies differ between ecosystems. 10% is a stated assumption.
Much of the energy is used by the organisms or disperses as heat.

questions.prompt: A fourth level is three steps above producers. From 8000 kJ with an assumed 10% transfer at each step, how many kJ reach level 4?
hints: Count the number of transfers.
Apply the efficiency once for each transfer.
Track the sequence step by step.
questions.onCorrect: 8 kJ. Three transfers at 10% leave one thousandth of the starting energy.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the energy at level 3. One more transfer is needed.
That is the energy at level 2. Two more transfers are needed.

questions.prompt: A population starts at 10 and doubles each round. What is it after three rounds?
hints: Double once per round.
After two rounds there are 40.
Double once more.
questions.onCorrect: 80. Each round doubles the last, so the increases grow larger.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 10 each round. Each round doubles instead.
That is the count after only two rounds.

questions.prompt: Name the population limit approached in a simple logistic model under fixed environmental conditions.
hints: Competition for resources lowers net growth near this level.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Carrying capacity reflects the population supported by those conditions.

questions.onCorrect: Carrying capacity. Growth levels off near the size the habitat can support.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are rates. The question asks for the size the habitat can support.

questions.prompt: A closed population has 12 births and 12 deaths in one interval. What is its net change?
hints: Gains add and losses subtract.
There is no migration in this closed population.
Subtract the deaths from the births.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 12 − 12 = 0, although individuals were born and died.

questions.onCorrect: Zero. Births and deaths balance, so the size is steady even though individuals come and go.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the births and deaths together. Deaths take away from the population.
That is the births alone. Take the deaths away.

questions.prompt: After a drought reduces the food supply, what may happen to the carrying capacity?
hints: The environment has changed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Carrying capacity depends on environmental resources and conditions.

choices.label: It becomes the same for every species

questions.onCorrect: It can decrease. Carrying capacity depends on conditions, so it is not a fixed number.

misconceptions.feedback: It depends on resources, and a drought changes them.
Each species needs different resources, so each has its own limit.

questions.prompt: A closed population starts at 70, with 16 births and 9 deaths. What is its final size?
hints: Start with the original population.
Add the births.
Subtract the deaths.
questions.onCorrect: 77. Net change is births minus deaths, added to the starting size.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the deaths. Subtract them.
That subtracts the births and adds nothing. Births add to the population.

questions.prompt: Does a smooth logistic curve predict every fluctuation in a wild population?
hints: Identify the processes the model omits.

acceptedIdeas: No, weather, interactions and chance can cause departures
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The curve is a simplified model; real populations can fluctuate or overshoot.

choices.label: Only for populations above one million
No, weather, interactions and chance can cause departures

questions.onCorrect: No. The curve is a simplified model, and weather, interactions and chance shift real numbers.

misconceptions.feedback: A smooth curve leaves out weather, disease and chance.
Population size does not make a model exact.

questions.prompt: A claim says fertiliser helps plants grow. Name the quantity you would measure to test it.
hints: Choose something you can measure with a ruler over a set time.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A defined measurable outcome, such as change in height over a set time, allows a reproducible comparison.

questions.onCorrect: Height, or its change over a set time. A measurable outcome makes the claim testable.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a judgement, not a measurement. Pick something you could record with a ruler.

questions.prompt: Group A grows from 10 cm to 16 cm. How much does its mean height increase, in cm?
hints: Use the same group's baseline.
Subtract the starting height from the final height.
Take the starting height off the final height.
questions.onCorrect: 6 cm. Growth is the final height minus the baseline.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the final height. Subtract the starting height.
That adds the heights. Growth is the change, so subtract.

questions.prompt: Comparable pots are allocated to fertiliser or control by chance. Name this allocation method.
hints: Name how treatments are given out, not how often height is measured.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Random assignment reduces systematic group differences; independent pots provide replication.

questions.onCorrect: Random assignment. Chance spreads other differences evenly between the groups.

misconceptions.feedback: Replication means using many independent pots. This question asks how treatments are given out.

questions.prompt: Taller plants occur at wetter sites. What follows from that observation alone?
hints: A correlation does not isolate a cause.

acceptedIdeas: Rainfall and height are associated, but other causes need checking
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The association could reflect rainfall, soil or other related factors.

choices.label: Rainfall is proven to be the only cause
Rainfall and height are associated, but other causes need checking

questions.onCorrect: The two are associated. Other factors, such as soil, could explain the pattern.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing was controlled, so other causes cannot be ruled out.
Nothing links plant height to rainfall in that direction.

questions.prompt: A treated group increases by 9 cm and its matched control by 6 cm. What is the difference in growth, in cm?
hints: Compare changes over the same interval.
Use growth, not final height.
Subtract the control's growth from the treated group's.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 9 − 6 = 3 cm greater growth in the treated group.

questions.onCorrect: 3 cm. Subtract the control's growth to see the effect of the treatment.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two growths. Compare them by subtracting.
That is the treated group's growth alone. Take the control's growth away.

questions.prompt: Why report variability across independent pots as well as the mean?
hints: An average alone does not show the spread.

acceptedIdeas: It shows how consistent the results are
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Variability reveals whether the mean hides wide differences between replicates.

choices.label: It shows how consistent the results are
It proves every plant behaves identically

questions.onCorrect: It shows how consistent the results are. A mean can hide wide differences between pots.

misconceptions.feedback: A control is still needed to compare against. Variability tells you about consistency.
Variability shows the opposite: how much the plants differ.

questions.prompt: An old strand reads ATGC. Write the bases of the new strand built against it, in the same left-to-right order.
hints: Pair each base in turn.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A pairs with T, T with A, G with C, and C with G, giving TACG.

questions.onCorrect: TACG. Each old base fixes its partner, so the new strand is fully determined.

misconceptions.feedback: That repeats the old strand. Write each base's partner.
That reverses the order. Keep the new bases in step with the old ones.

questions.prompt: A template strand has 40 bases. How many bases are in the new strand built against it?
hints: How many partners does each template base get?
Each base gets one partner.
The new strand is the same length as the template.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each template base gets exactly one partner, so the new strand also has 40 bases.

questions.onCorrect: 40. Every template base gets exactly one partner, so the strands match in length.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts both strands together. The question asks about the new strand only.
Nothing halves the length. Each template base still gets a partner.

questions.prompt: How many of the four strips in the new zipped pairs are brand new?
hints: The old strips are not thrown away. What happens to them?
Each old strip is given one new partner.
Count the new partners.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The two old strips are kept. Each gets one new partner, so two of the four strips are new.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Each pair keeps one old strip and gains one new one. DNA copying works the same way.

misconceptions.feedback: Two of the four are the old strips, which were kept.
Each old strip gets its own new partner, so there is more than one new strip.

questions.prompt: What makes a DNA strand a template?
hints: Think about what decides each new base.

acceptedIdeas: Its base order fixes the base order of its partner
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Because of base pairing, each base in the strand fixes the base opposite it.

choices.label: Its base order fixes the base order of its partner
It is always the longer strand
It can be read only from the left

questions.onCorrect: Its base order fixes its partner's. Each base allows only one partner.

misconceptions.feedback: Both strands are the same length. What matters is the order of their bases.
A strand can serve as a template at any point along its length.

questions.prompt: What are the two joined copies of a replicated chromosome called?
hints: The name includes a family relationship.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A replicated chromosome has two sister chromatids.

questions.onCorrect: Sister chromatids. They are identical copies that stay joined until the cell divides.

misconceptions.feedback: Homologous chromosomes come from different parents. These copies came from one chromosome.

questions.prompt: A membrane is permeable to water but not to a dye. 9 dye units are on the left and 3 on the right. How many dye units are on the left after a long time?
hints: Which substances can cross this membrane?
Can the dye cross?
If the dye cannot move, its amounts stay as they began.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The dye cannot cross, so its amounts do not change: 9 on the left.

questions.onCorrect: 9. The dye cannot cross, so a concentration difference moves nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what each side would hold if the dye could cross. Check what the membrane lets through.
That's the right side's amount. Ask about the left.

questions.prompt: After a long time, how many people are in the left room?
hints: Does anyone leave the building, or arrive?
Count everyone in both rooms together.
Think about sharing that crowd between two equal rooms.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Everyone is still in the building: 20 + 4 = 24. Equal rooms end up with equal crowds: 24 ÷ 2 = 12.

questions.onCorrect: 12. People cross both ways, but more leave the crowded room, so the rooms settle at equal numbers.

misconceptions.feedback: That's where the left room started. People keep crossing the door, so the count changes.
That's everyone in the building. The question asks about the left room only.

questions.prompt: Dye is dropped into still water. Overall, where does the dye move?
hints: Which region sends more particles across the boundary between them?

acceptedIdeas: From where it is crowded to where it is not
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Net movement runs from the more concentrated region to the less concentrated one.

choices.label: From where it is crowded to where it is not
From where it is sparse to where it is crowded

questions.onCorrect: From crowded to sparse. More particles cross that way, so the net movement follows.

misconceptions.feedback: That would make the crowd even more crowded. More particles leave the crowded region than enter it.
Particles move constantly. It is the net movement that settles down, not the particles.

questions.prompt: Why does the total stay the same while solute moves?
hints: Think about where each particle goes.

acceptedIdeas: Solute only moves from place to place; none is made or lost
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Diffusion moves solute between compartments but does not create or destroy it.

choices.label: Solute only moves from place to place; none is made or lost
Solute is replaced from outside the compartments
The two sides swap their solute exactly

questions.onCorrect: Diffusion only moves solute around. The total is conserved, so you can add the sides first.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing arrives from outside this closed system.
The sides don't swap. Net movement stops once the concentrations match.

questions.prompt: What word describes a membrane that lets a substance cross?
hints: The word starts with per-, meaning through.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A membrane is permeable to a substance if the substance can cross it.

questions.onCorrect: Permeable. Always check what a membrane is permeable to before predicting movement.

misconceptions.feedback: Impermeable means the opposite: nothing can cross.

questions.prompt: Three independent treated pots grow 7 cm, 9 cm and 11 cm. What is the mean growth, in cm?
hints: Add the three growths.
Divide the total by the number of pots.
Share the total equally between the pots.
questions.onCorrect: 9 cm. The mean is the total divided by the number of independent pots.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total. Divide it by the number of pots.
That is the largest value. The mean uses every pot.

questions.prompt: A researcher gives fertiliser only to the plants that already look healthiest. Name the feature of a fair test that this breaks.
hints: How should treatments be given out?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Choosing the healthiest plants for the treatment builds a systematic difference into the groups.

questions.onCorrect: Random assignment. Picking the healthiest plants builds in a difference that has nothing to do with the fertiliser.

misconceptions.feedback: There may still be a control. The problem is how the plants were chosen for each group.
The number of plants is not the problem. The choice of which get the treatment is.

questions.prompt: How many more centimetres did plant A grow than plant B?
hints: Growth is the change in height, not the final height.
Work out each plant's growth separately.
Subtract plant B's growth from plant A's.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Plant A grew 19 − 4 = 15 cm. Plant B grew 22 − 12 = 10 cm. The difference is 5 cm.

questions.onCorrect: 5 cm. Compare how much each plant grew, because the plants did not start at the same height.

misconceptions.feedback: That compares the final heights, but B ended taller. Compare how much each plant grew.
That is plant A's growth alone. Subtract plant B's growth from it.

questions.prompt: Why compare each group's change instead of its final height?
hints: Think about where each group began.

acceptedIdeas: The groups started at different heights
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Groups that start at different heights can mislead if only final height is compared.

choices.label: The groups started at different heights
Change is always larger than final height

questions.onCorrect: The groups started at different heights, so only each group's change shows how much it grew.

misconceptions.feedback: Final heights can be measured. They just do not show how much each group grew.
Size does not decide which measure is fairer. The starting point does.

questions.prompt: Level 3 holds 50 kJ and the transfer efficiency is 10%. How many kJ did level 2 hold?
hints: The level below holds more than the level above.
The output is one tenth of the input.
Divide by the efficiency as a decimal.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Level 2 held 50 ÷ 0.10 = 500 kJ.

questions.onCorrect: 500 kJ. Undo a 10% transfer by dividing by the efficiency.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the efficiency, which goes forwards. Work backwards by dividing.
That adds a tenth back on. Divide to undo the transfer.

questions.prompt: Producers hold 6000 kJ and the transfer efficiency is 10% at each step. How many kJ reach level 3?
hints: Level 3 is two steps above the producers.
Apply the efficiency once for each step.
Take a tenth, then a tenth of that.
questions.onCorrect: 60 kJ. Two transfers at 10% leave a hundredth of the starting energy.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the energy at level 2. One more transfer is needed.
That takes a tenth three times. Level 3 needs only two transfers.

questions.prompt: How many kilograms of grain does the farmer feed for each kilogram of body mass the cow gains?
hints: Compare the grain fed with the mass gained.
How many times does the gain fit into the grain?
Divide the grain by the mass gained.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 kg of grain ÷ 10 kg gained = 10 kg of grain per kg gained.

questions.onCorrect: 10 kg of grain for every kg gained. Most of what an animal eats does not become new body mass.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the amount that did not become body mass. The question asks for grain per kilogram gained.
That adds the grain and the gain. Compare them by dividing.

questions.prompt: Why is the second 10% taken from the energy at level 2 and not from the original amount?
hints: Each transfer moves energy from one level to the next.

acceptedIdeas: Each transfer starts from the energy that reached the level it leaves
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The second transfer passes on a share of what level 2 holds.

choices.label: Each transfer starts from the energy that reached the level it leaves
The original amount is no longer counted
Level 2 gains extra energy from the sun

questions.onCorrect: Each step passes on a share of what that level holds, so the shares multiply.

misconceptions.feedback: The original energy is still the source. It has just been reduced by the first transfer.
In this accounting nothing new enters at level 2.

questions.prompt: An enzyme sample makes 9 units of product per minute and its control makes 3 per minute. After 5 minutes, how many more units has the enzyme sample made?
hints: Find how much faster the enzyme sample goes each minute.
Multiply that difference by the number of minutes.
Subtract the rates first, then use 5 minutes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The rates differ by 9 − 3 = 6 per minute. Over 5 minutes: 6 × 5 = 30 more units.

questions.onCorrect: 30 more units. The rates differ by a steady amount, so the gap grows with time.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the enzyme sample's whole output. Compare it with the control's.
That's the gap after one minute. Run it for five.

questions.prompt: How many times faster is beaker B?
hints: Compare the two rates.
How many lots of 4 make 12?
Divide the faster rate by the slower one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 12 ÷ 4 = 3, so beaker B is three times as fast.

questions.onCorrect: 3 times. The helper changes how fast the reaction runs, and enzymes do exactly that.

misconceptions.feedback: That's how much more B makes each minute. 'Times faster' compares by dividing.
That adds the two rates. Compare them by dividing.

questions.prompt: Enzyme A speeds up as it is warmed from 10°C to 40°C. Predict what happens to its rate at 55°C: does it rise, fall or stay the same?
hints: Think about what too much heat does to a protein.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At 55°C the rate falls because heat changes the enzyme's shape.

questions.onCorrect: It falls. Warming helps up to a point, then heat damages the enzyme.

misconceptions.feedback: Warmth speeds particles up, but there is a limit. Past it, the enzyme itself is affected.
The rate keeps changing with temperature. Predict which way.

questions.prompt: Name the part of an enzyme where the substrate binds.
hints: It is the part whose shape fits the substrate.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The substrate binds at the enzyme's active site.

questions.onCorrect: The active site. Its shape fits the substrate, and heat that changes the shape stops the fit.

misconceptions.feedback: The substrate is the molecule that binds. Name the place on the enzyme where it binds.

questions.prompt: Why can't we say that 40°C is the best temperature for every enzyme?
hints: Think about the enzyme's shape.

acceptedIdeas: Each enzyme has its own shape, so its best range can differ
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The best temperature depends on the enzyme, and the data only cover the temperatures that were measured.

choices.label: Every enzyme works best at the same temperature
Each enzyme has its own shape, so its best range can differ

questions.onCorrect: Each enzyme has its own shape, so its best range differs. Data show only the temperatures tested.

misconceptions.feedback: The two enzymes on the screen do not peak together.
Temperature changes rate in all of these data sets.

questions.prompt: Not all the energy from fuel ends up in ATP. In what form does much of the rest disperse?
hints: Think about why your body is warm.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Energy that is not transferred to ATP disperses as heat.

questions.onCorrect: Heat. Some energy always disperses as heat, which is why living things are warm.

misconceptions.feedback: Most cells give out very little light. Think about what a warm body gives off.

questions.prompt: A cell completely oxidises five glucose molecules. How many carbon atoms end up in CO₂?
hints: How many carbon atoms does one glucose have?
All the carbon from the fuel ends up in CO₂.
Multiply the carbon atoms in one glucose by five.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each glucose has six carbon atoms, and all of them end up in CO₂: 5 × 6 = 30.

questions.onCorrect: 30. Carbon is conserved, so every carbon atom in the fuel ends up in CO₂.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the carbon in one glucose. There are five.
That counts the glucose molecules. Count the carbon atoms in them.

questions.prompt: Which gas do you breathe out that comes from this process?
hints: It is also what a candle gives out.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Cells release carbon dioxide when they use sugar as fuel.

questions.onCorrect: Carbon dioxide. Cells use sugar and oxygen, and carbon dioxide is one of the products.

misconceptions.feedback: Oxygen is what the cells use up. Name the gas they give out.

questions.prompt: Why can you count the CO₂ by counting the carbon atoms in the fuel?
hints: Think about what happens to atoms in any chemical reaction.

acceptedIdeas: Carbon atoms are rearranged into the products, not destroyed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Atoms are conserved, so the carbon from the fuel ends up in the products.

choices.label: Carbon atoms are rearranged into the products, not destroyed
Carbon atoms are turned into energy

questions.onCorrect: Atoms are conserved. The carbon is rearranged into CO₂, so the counts match.

misconceptions.feedback: Energy and atoms are different things. Atoms are never turned into energy in a cell.
Oxygen is a reactant here, but the carbon comes from the fuel.

questions.prompt: A blank jar with no organisms also loses 2 units of oxygen in the same three minutes, while the organism jar loses 9. How many units did the organisms themselves use?
hints: Some oxygen is lost even without organisms.
The blank shows the loss that is not the organisms' doing.
Take the blank's loss off the organisms' jar.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 9 − 2 = 7 units. The blank's loss is not the organisms' doing.

questions.onCorrect: 7 units. The blank shows the loss due to the apparatus, so subtract it to isolate the organisms.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the organism jar's total loss. Part of it also happens in the blank.
That adds the two losses. The blank's loss should come off.

questions.prompt: A cell has a plasma membrane and DNA, but no nucleus and no mitochondria. What kind of cell is it?
hints: Which cell type keeps its DNA in a nucleoid?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No nucleus and no organelles is the bacterial design.

questions.onCorrect: A bacterium. No nucleus and no mitochondria is the bacterial design.

misconceptions.feedback: Animal and plant cells have a nucleus and mitochondria. This cell has neither.

questions.prompt: What should a cell's outer boundary be like?
hints: What would happen to the food if nothing could get in?

acceptedIdeas: A skin that lets some things through and keeps others out
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A cell needs a boundary that lets some things through and keeps others out.

choices.label: A sealed wall that lets nothing through
A skin that lets some things through and keeps others out
No boundary, so the cell mixes with its surroundings

questions.onCorrect: A boundary that lets some things through and holds others back. Cells have exactly that.

misconceptions.feedback: A sealed wall would starve the cell and trap its waste.
Without a boundary the cell's contents would drift away and its chemistry would fall apart.

questions.prompt: A cell keeps its DNA inside a nucleus. What kind of cell is it?
hints: Animal and plant cells are this kind.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A cell with a nucleus is eukaryotic.

questions.onCorrect: Eukaryotic. A nucleus holding the DNA is the mark of a eukaryotic cell.

misconceptions.feedback: Bacteria have no nucleus. Look for the cell type that does.

questions.prompt: What does the nucleus's own membrane do for the DNA?
hints: Think about what a membrane does for any compartment.

acceptedIdeas: It keeps most of the DNA enclosed in one compartment
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The nuclear membrane encloses most of the DNA in one compartment.

choices.label: It keeps most of the DNA enclosed in one compartment
It makes the DNA copy itself faster
It turns the DNA into protein

questions.onCorrect: It encloses the DNA. A membrane-bound compartment is what makes a nucleus a nucleus.

misconceptions.feedback: Copying is done by enzymes. The membrane's job is to enclose.
Proteins are built elsewhere in the cell. The nucleus holds the DNA that carries their instructions.

questions.prompt: Which organelle captures light energy in a leaf cell?
hints: Leaf cells are green because of it.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Chloroplasts capture light energy.

questions.onCorrect: The chloroplast. It captures light energy for photosynthesis.

misconceptions.feedback: Mitochondria work with fuel, not light.

questions.prompt: A plant is given CO₂ whose carbon atoms are labelled. Name the kind of molecule the labelled carbon ends up in.
hints: Where does the carbon from CO₂ go?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The carbon from CO₂ is built into sugar such as glucose.

questions.onCorrect: Sugar. The carbon from CO₂ is built into glucose, so the label follows the carbon.

misconceptions.feedback: Oxygen is released as a product, and it comes from water. The label rides on carbon.

questions.prompt: A leaf makes four glucose molecules. How many water molecules does that use, using the simplified equation?
hints: Read the number in front of H₂O.
That number is for one glucose.
Multiply by four glucose molecules.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each glucose uses six H₂O: 4 × 6 = 24.

questions.onCorrect: 24. Six water molecules go in for each glucose, so scale by the number made.

misconceptions.feedback: That is for one glucose. There are four.
That counts the glucose molecules. Multiply by the water used for each.

questions.prompt: Where did nearly all of the tree's new mass come from?
hints: How much mass did the soil lose compared with the tree's gain?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Most of a tree's new mass is built from carbon dioxide in the air and from water.

questions.onCorrect: The air and water. Plants build their bodies from carbon dioxide and water, not from the soil.

misconceptions.feedback: The soil lost almost nothing, so it cannot account for such a large gain.
Light carries energy, but it adds no atoms to the tree.

questions.prompt: In the overall equation, how many CO₂ molecules go in for one glucose molecule?
hints: Read the number written in front of CO₂.
Find CO₂ on the left-hand side of the equation.
It matches the number of carbon atoms in glucose.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The equation starts 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + light, so six CO₂ per glucose.

questions.onCorrect: Six. One glucose has six carbon atoms, and each CO₂ brings one.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one glucose. Read the number in front of CO₂.
That is the number of hydrogen atoms in glucose. Read the number in front of CO₂.

questions.prompt: Why does the number of CO₂ molecules equal the number of carbon atoms in the sugar?
hints: Count the carbon atoms inside one CO₂.

acceptedIdeas: Each CO₂ supplies exactly one carbon atom
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each CO₂ contains one carbon atom, and every carbon atom in the sugar came from one.

choices.label: Light supplies the rest of the carbon
Each CO₂ supplies exactly one carbon atom

questions.onCorrect: Each CO₂ carries one carbon atom, so counting carbon atoms counts CO₂ molecules.

misconceptions.feedback: Light is energy and has no atoms.
Water contains hydrogen and oxygen only. The carbon comes from the gas.

questions.prompt: A human gamete has 23 chromosomes. How many chromosomes does a human body cell have?
hints: A gamete holds one set.
A body cell holds two sets.
Double the gamete's number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A body cell is diploid, with two sets: 2 × 23 = 46.

questions.onCorrect: 46. A body cell is diploid, so it holds twice the number a gamete holds.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one set. A body cell has two.
That doubles twice. A body cell holds just two sets.

questions.prompt: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes. What does meiosis II separate?
hints: Think of the two joined copies of each chromosome.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Meiosis II separates sister chromatids.

questions.onCorrect: Sister chromatids. They are the joined copies made before meiosis I.

misconceptions.feedback: Those were already separated in meiosis I. Name the structures that remain joined.

questions.prompt: A diploid cell has 12 chromosomes. How many chromosomes does each gamete made from it have?
hints: A gamete holds one chromosome set.
The diploid cell holds two sets.
Halve the diploid number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A gamete is haploid, with half the diploid number: 12 ÷ 2 = 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Meiosis halves the number so each gamete has one set.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the diploid number. A gamete holds half of it.
That halves twice. Meiosis halves the number once overall.

questions.prompt: How many chromosomes does the egg carry?
hints: Each parent supplies the same number.
The two contributions must add up to the baby's total.
Share the baby's total equally between egg and sperm.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The egg and sperm each supply half of 46: 46 ÷ 2 = 23.

questions.onCorrect: 23. Gametes carry half the usual number, so that fertilisation restores the full number.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the full number. If the egg carried 46 and the sperm carried 46, the baby would have double.
That is what you would get if both gametes carried a full set.

questions.prompt: Why does the chromosome number halve in meiosis I and not in meiosis II?
hints: Think about which relationship is separated in each division.

acceptedIdeas: Homologous chromosomes go to different cells in meiosis I
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: In meiosis I each daughter gets one chromosome from each homologous pair, so the number halves.

choices.label: Meiosis II copies the DNA again
Homologous chromosomes go to different cells in meiosis I
DNA is destroyed in meiosis I

questions.onCorrect: Each cell gets one chromosome from each pair in meiosis I. Meiosis II only separates the copies.

misconceptions.feedback: There is no second copying. Meiosis II divides the existing copies.
No DNA is destroyed. Each chromosome goes to one daughter cell.

questions.prompt: After replication, a cell has 10 DNA molecules. How many chromosomes does it have?
hints: How many DNA molecules does one replicated chromosome hold?
Each replicated chromosome has two chromatids.
Share the DNA molecules out two to a chromosome.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each chromosome now holds two DNA molecules, so 10 ÷ 2 = 5 chromosomes.

questions.onCorrect: 5. Two DNA molecules per replicated chromosome, so halve the count of DNA molecules.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of DNA molecules. Two of them make up each chromosome.
Replication has already happened. Work back from the DNA molecules.

questions.prompt: One cell completes four ideal rounds of division, with every descendant dividing each round. How many cells result?
hints: Double once for each round.
Three rounds give eight cells.
Double the count once more.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sequence is 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16.

questions.onCorrect: 16. Four rounds make four doublings.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count after three rounds. There is one more.
That counts the rounds. Each round doubles the cell count.

questions.prompt: How many pages does each student receive?
hints: Each student gets a whole set, not part of one.
How many pages are in one set?
The copy is as long as the original.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each student gets one complete set, which has 5 pages.

questions.onCorrect: 5. Each side gets a full set. Dividing cells copy their chromosomes before sharing them out.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total number of pages. Each student gets one set only.
That counts the students. The question asks about pages.

questions.prompt: Why does each sister chromatid count as one DNA molecule?
hints: What did replication copy?

acceptedIdeas: It is one copy of the chromosome's DNA
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each chromatid is one complete copy of the chromosome's DNA molecule.

choices.label: It is one copy of the chromosome's DNA
It is half a DNA molecule
It is a protein, not DNA

questions.onCorrect: Each chromatid is one complete copy. Two chromatids mean two DNA molecules.

misconceptions.feedback: Replication makes complete copies, not halves.
Chromatids are made of DNA with its proteins. The DNA is what is counted.

questions.prompt: A tissue has 8 cells. In one round only half of them divide, and each of those becomes two cells. How many cells are there after that round?
hints: How many cells divide?
Each dividing cell becomes two, a gain of one.
Add the gain to the cells you started with.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four cells divide into eight, and four do not: 8 + 4 = 12 cells.

questions.onCorrect: 12. Only the dividing cells add to the total, so regulated tissue grows more slowly than ideal doubling.

misconceptions.feedback: That doubles all the cells. Only half of them divide here.
That is the starting count. The dividing cells add to it.

questions.prompt: A gene has 600 bases. A single substitution changes one of them. How many bases does the mutated gene have?
hints: Does a substitution add or remove any base?
One base is swapped for another.
The length stays as it was.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A substitution swaps one base for another, so the length is unchanged: 600 bases.

questions.onCorrect: 600. A substitution swaps a base without changing the length.

misconceptions.feedback: A substitution does not remove a base. It swaps one.
A substitution does not add a base. It swaps one.

questions.prompt: A mutation arises in one of a parent's skin cells. What is the likely result for the parent's children?
hints: Which cells pass DNA to children?

acceptedIdeas: They do not inherit it, because it is not in a gamete
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A mutation confined to an ordinary body cell generally does not reach offspring.

choices.label: They do not inherit it, because it is not in a gamete
They inherit it only if it is harmful

questions.onCorrect: They do not inherit it. Only a mutation in a gamete's line of cells can be passed on.

misconceptions.feedback: Skin cells do not pass DNA to the next generation.
Harm does not decide inheritance. Which cells carry the mutation does.

questions.prompt: Compare the aligned sequences ACGTAC and TCGAAG. How many positions differ?
hints: Align the sequences and keep them in step.
Compare each of the six pairs in turn.
Count only the pairs that disagree.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Positions 1, 4 and 6 differ; the other three agree.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Positions 1, 4 and 6 differ, so three bases have changed.

misconceptions.feedback: There is another mismatch. Check every position.
That is the length of the sequences. Count only the mismatches.

questions.prompt: How many slips are on the page, on average?
hints: How many hundreds of words are on the page?
There is one slip for each hundred words.
Divide the page length by the words per slip.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 500 words ÷ 100 words per slip = 5 slips.

questions.onCorrect: 5. Even careful copying makes errors at a steady rate, and copying DNA is no different.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many words go by between slips. Count the slips on the whole page.
That is the slips in a single hundred words. The page has more words than that.

questions.prompt: What can you conclude from a single DNA substitution alone?
hints: A changed letter does not specify a trait.

acceptedIdeas: Its biological effect needs additional evidence
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Effects depend on sequence context and environment; some substitutions have little detectable effect.

choices.label: Its biological effect needs additional evidence

questions.onCorrect: Its effect needs more evidence. A changed base may be harmful, helpful or make no difference.

misconceptions.feedback: Many substitutions have little or no effect, so harm cannot be assumed.
Some help, but a change alone does not show that.

questions.prompt: Do mutations arise because an organism needs them? Answer yes or no.
hints: Think about the scribe's slips. Did the scribe choose them?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Mutations arise by chance. Need does not direct them.

questions.onCorrect: No. Mutations arise at random, whether or not they would help.

misconceptions.feedback: Mutations arise by chance. An organism's needs do not steer them.

questions.prompt: Natural selection acts only on differences that pass from parents to offspring. What word describes such differences?
hints: The word comes from inherit.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Heritable differences can be passed on, so selection can change their frequency.

questions.onCorrect: Heritable. A difference that is not passed on cannot change the next generation.

misconceptions.feedback: Traits gained during a lifetime are not passed on in the way selection needs.

questions.prompt: How many green beetles are left?
hints: Only the green beetles are eaten.
The birds eat half of them.
Halve the number of green beetles.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Half of 16 is 8, so 8 green beetles remain.

questions.onCorrect: 8. One colour is removed faster than the other, so the colours' shares of the population will shift.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many green beetles there were before the birds ate any.
That takes half of the whole meadow. The birds ate only half of the green beetles.

questions.prompt: Why compare percentages instead of counts when the population size changes?
hints: What happens to a count if the population doubles?

acceptedIdeas: A count changes with the size of the population, but a frequency does not
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A frequency is a share of the whole, so it can be compared between populations of different sizes.

choices.label: A count changes with the size of the population, but a frequency does not
Percentages are always larger than counts

questions.onCorrect: A share of the whole stays comparable when the population size changes.

misconceptions.feedback: Size has nothing to do with which number is larger. The point is what each one measures.
Counts can be added. The problem is comparing populations of different sizes.

questions.prompt: In environment B, green beetles fall from 20 of 40 to 8 of 40. What percentage of the beetles is green afterwards?
hints: Use the green count divided by the total.
The total is still the same number of beetles.
Convert the fraction to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: 20%. In this environment green does worse, so its share falls.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count. Convert it into a share of the total.
That is the share that is not green.

questions.prompt: A closed population starts at 120, with 30 births and 45 deaths. What is its final size?
hints: Start with the original population.
Add the births.
Subtract the deaths.
questions.onCorrect: 105. Deaths outnumbered births, so the population fell.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the deaths. Subtract them.
That adds the deaths. Deaths reduce the population.

questions.prompt: A population of 6 doubles every round with no limit. How many are there after four rounds?
hints: Double once for each round.
After three rounds there are 48.
Double once more.
questions.onCorrect: 96. Four doublings multiply the starting number by 16.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 6 each round. Doubling multiplies instead.
That is the count after only three rounds.

questions.prompt: On which day from today does the patch first cover more than 20 square metres?
hints: Write the area for each day: it doubles every time.
Keep doubling until the area passes the pond's size.
Check the area on day four, then on the day after.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The area is 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 on days 0 to 4, and 32 on day 5, which is over 20.

questions.onCorrect: Day 5. Doubling is slow at first and then very fast, because each increase is bigger than the last.

misconceptions.feedback: On that day the patch covers 16 square metres, which is still under 20.
That is the pond's size in square metres. The question asks for a day.

questions.prompt: Real populations cannot double forever. As a habitat becomes crowded, what happens to the population's growth each round: does it speed up, stay the same or slow down?
hints: Think about food and space as numbers rise.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Crowding lowers births or raises deaths, so growth slows.

questions.onCorrect: It slows down. Crowding cuts births or raises deaths, so each round adds less.

misconceptions.feedback: More individuals share the same food and space, which makes things harder, not easier.
Competition changes births and deaths as numbers rise, so the growth does not stay fixed.

questions.prompt: Why is this population called closed?
hints: Think about what could change the number besides births and deaths.

acceptedIdeas: Individuals enter or leave only by birth and death
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A closed population has no migration, so only births and deaths change its size.

choices.label: Individuals enter or leave only by birth and death
It lives in a closed jar

questions.onCorrect: No one arrives or leaves. Only births and deaths change the size.

misconceptions.feedback: Deaths do occur. A closed population just has no migration.
Closed describes movement of individuals, not the container.

questions.prompt: For Aa × Aa, what percentage of offspring is expected to show the dominant phenotype?
hints: List the four pairings.
Which genotypes show the dominant trait?
Count those boxes out of four.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: AA, Aa and Aa show the dominant trait: 3 ÷ 4 = 75%.

questions.onCorrect: 75%. AA and Aa both show the dominant trait, and together they fill three boxes of four.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance of aa only. Count every genotype that shows the dominant trait.
That counts Aa alone. AA shows the dominant trait too.

questions.prompt: Two parents both show the dominant trait, but their child shows the recessive trait. What word describes each parent's genotype?
hints: The child must have received a recessive allele from each parent.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each parent must carry one recessive allele without showing it, so each is heterozygous.

questions.onCorrect: Heterozygous. Each parent hid a recessive allele and passed it on.

misconceptions.feedback: A parent with two dominant alleles could not pass on a recessive one.

questions.prompt: What is the chance, as a percentage, that both coins land heads?
hints: Write out every combination of the two coins.
There are four equally likely combinations.
How many of those four have two heads?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The four equally likely outcomes are HH, HT, TH and TT. One of the four is HH: 1 ÷ 4 = 25%.

questions.onCorrect: 25%. List the equally likely outcomes and count the ones you want. A cross works the same way.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance for one coin. Both coins must land heads.
Each coin could land tails, so both heads is not certain.

questions.prompt: How many boxes does the Punnett square for Aa × Aa have?
hints: Each parent makes two kinds of gamete.
Each box pairs one gamete from each parent.
Multiply the kinds of gamete from the two parents.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each parent makes two kinds of gamete, so there are 2 × 2 = 4 pairings.

questions.onCorrect: 4. Two kinds of gamete from each parent make four equally likely pairings.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the kinds of gamete from one parent. The square pairs gametes from both.
Every pairing of the two parents' gametes gets a box, and that is more than three.

questions.prompt: Why does Aa fill two boxes in the Aa × Aa square?
hints: Think about which parent gives which allele.

acceptedIdeas: A and a can meet in either order, so two boxes give Aa
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The Aa genotype can be made in two ways, so it fills two of the four boxes.

choices.label: Aa is more likely because it is dominant
A and a can meet in either order, so two boxes give Aa

questions.onCorrect: There are two ways to make Aa, so it fills two of the four boxes.

misconceptions.feedback: Dominance affects the trait you see. It does not change how often a genotype forms.
Both boxes are correct. Each shows a different way to make the same genotype.

questions.prompt: In a food web an arrow points from a rabbit to a fox. Which organism is the consumer?
hints: Which way does an arrow point?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The arrow runs from food to consumer, so the fox eats the rabbit.

questions.onCorrect: The fox. The arrow points to the eater.

misconceptions.feedback: The arrow starts at the food. The rabbit is being eaten here.

questions.prompt: Which kind of organism returns matter from dead material to the soil and water so that producers can use it again?
hints: They break down dead organisms.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Decomposers return matter from dead material to environmental pools.

questions.onCorrect: Decomposers. They recycle matter, though energy is not recycled with it.

misconceptions.feedback: Producers use the recycled matter. Another group returns it.

questions.prompt: What happens to the amount of algae at first?
hints: Who was eating the algae?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With fewer zooplankton eating it, the algae increases at first.

questions.onCorrect: It increases. Fewer eaters mean less algae is eaten, which is how links in a web connect.

misconceptions.feedback: The algae's eaters were killed. Less of it is being eaten, not more.

questions.prompt: Why do all the routes in a web trace back to a producer?
hints: Where does the first food in the web come from?

acceptedIdeas: Producers are the only organisms that make their own food, so every other organism depends on them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only producers make their own food, so every consumer's energy traces back to them.

choices.label: Producers are the only organisms that make their own food, so every other organism depends on them
Producers are always the largest organisms
Producers eat all the other organisms

questions.onCorrect: Producers make their own food. Every consumer's energy comes from them, directly or not.

misconceptions.feedback: Size does not decide it. Grass and algae are producers because they make their own food.
Producers are not eaters. The arrows run from them to the consumers.

questions.prompt: Water can cross but solute cannot. Equal volumes at equal pressure hold 9 solute units on the left and 3 on the right. Which side gains water at first?
hints: Which side is more concentrated?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The left side has more solute, so it gains water.

questions.onCorrect: The left side. It is the more concentrated, so water moves toward it.

misconceptions.feedback: The right side has less solute. Water moves toward more solute.

questions.prompt: A compartment of volume 4 holds 20 units of trapped solute. Water leaves until its volume is 2. What is its concentration now?
hints: Water leaving does not take solute with it.
Keep the amount of solute unchanged.
Divide the amount by the new volume.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The solute stays at 20: 20 ÷ 2 = 10 units per volume.

questions.onCorrect: 10 per volume. Losing water with the same solute makes the solution more concentrated.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the concentration before water left. The volume is smaller now, so the solute is more crowded.

questions.prompt: How many spoonfuls of syrup are there per litre now?
hints: Water adds volume, not syrup.
How much syrup is there, and how many litres?
Divide the syrup by the litres.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The syrup is still 6 spoonfuls. 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 spoonfuls per litre.

questions.onCorrect: 1.5. Adding water spreads the same syrup through more volume, so the drink is weaker.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the strength before topping up. More water makes the drink weaker.
That's the total spoonfuls. The question asks how many per litre.

questions.prompt: You add water to a solution without adding any solute. Does it become more or less concentrated?
hints: The same solute is now spread through more volume.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same solute in more volume gives a lower concentration.

questions.onCorrect: Less concentrated. The same solute is spread through more volume.

misconceptions.feedback: Adding water adds volume but no solute, so the solute is more spread out.

questions.prompt: A compartment holds 20 solute units in volume 5. Water enters until its volume is 10. What is its concentration now?
hints: The solute cannot cross, so how much is there still?
Use the new volume, not the old one.
Divide the amount by the new volume.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The solute amount is unchanged: 20 ÷ 10 = 2 units per volume.

questions.onCorrect: 2 per volume. The amount stayed fixed while the volume doubled, so the concentration halved.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the concentration before water entered. Use the new volume.
